1. Electrostatics

Unit 1 · with Current Electricity 14 marks · charges and fields, Gauss, potential, capacitors

ConceptCharge, Coulomb’s law and superposition

  • Charge is quantised, q = ne with e = 1·6 × 10−19 C, and conserved in every process (pair production creates +e and −e together).
  • Coulomb: F = 14πε0q1q2r2 in vacuum; in a medium of dielectric constant K the force is F/K.
  • Compared with gravity: both inverse-square and central, but Coulomb force can repel, depends on the medium and is about 1036 times stronger between two protons.
  • Superposition: the force on one charge is the vector sum of the forces from each of the others, each computed as if the rest were absent.

Forces and fields add as vectors; potentials and energies add as scalars.

ConceptField lines and the dipole in a uniform field

  • E = F/q0; point charge E = kq/r2, radially out for +q, in for −q.
  • Lines start on +, end on −, never cross (one direction at a point), meet a conductor at 90°, and crowd where the field is strong. Between oppositely charged parallel plates they are straight, parallel and equally spaced: a uniform field.
  • Dipole moment p = q(2l), directed from −q to +q; unit C m.
  • In a uniform field the net force on a dipole is zero but there is a torque τ = p × E. In a non-uniform field there is a net force as well.

ConceptFlux and Gauss’s theorem

  • Flux φE = E·A = EA cos θ (θ between E and the normal); 0° gives EA, 90° gives 0, 180° gives −EA. Unit N m2 C−1 (= V m).
  • Gauss: the flux through any closed surface = qenc/ε0. It does not depend on the shape or size of the surface or on where the charge sits inside it, and charges outside contribute nothing (their lines go in and come out).
  • A dipole wholly inside a closed surface: net charge 0, so flux 0.
  • Essential properties of a Gaussian surface: it is closed; it passes through the point where E is wanted; and it is chosen by symmetry so that on each part E is constant and either normal or parallel to the surface.

Doubling the radius of the Gaussian surface leaves the flux unchanged; doubling the enclosed charge doubles it.

ConceptPotential, equipotentials and potential energy

  • V = W/q0 (work done bringing a unit + charge from infinity); point charge V = kq/r, positive for q > 0.
  • For several charges V is the algebraic sum. On the equatorial line of a dipole V = 0 everywhere, so no work is done moving a charge along it.
  • Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to E; closer spacing means a stronger field (E = −dV/dr). No work is done moving a charge on one.
  • Two charges: U = kq1q2/r. Three charges: sum over the three pairs. A charge in an external potential: U = qV.
  • Dipole in a uniform field: U = −p·E = −pE cos θ; minimum (stable) at 0°, zero at 90°, maximum at 180°.

ConceptConductors, capacitors and dielectrics

  • Inside a conductor in equilibrium E = 0, all excess charge sits on the outer surface, and the surface is an equipotential.
  • C = Q/V (farad). Parallel plates: C = ε0A/d; with a dielectric filling the gap C = Kε0A/d.
  • Energy (formula only, no derivation): U = ½CV2 = ½QV = Q2/2C; energy density ½ε0E2.
  • Dielectric inserted with the battery disconnected: Q fixed; C × K, V, E and U all ÷ K. With the battery connected: V fixed; C, Q and U all × K, E unchanged.
  • Polarisation: the dielectric’s induced surface charges set up a field opposing the applied one, which is why E and V fall.

Disconnected: Q is conserved. Connected: V is fixed by the battery. Decide which first.

DerivationField on the axial line of a dipole

Derive an expression for the electric field at a point on the axial line of an electric dipole. (S27 Q9(i), B26 Q9)

Charges −q at A and +q at B, AB = 2l. P lies on the axis at OP = r.

  1. Field of +q at P (distance r − l), away from B: E1 = kq/(r − l)2.
  2. Field of −q at P (distance r + l), towards A: E2 = kq/(r + l)2.
  3. They are along the same line and E1 > E2, so E = E1 − E2 = kq [(r+l)2 − (r−l)2] / (r2−l2)2.
  4. The bracket is 4rl, and q·2l = p.
Eaxial = 14πε02pr(r2 − l2)2 , along p   ⇒   for r >> l: E = 14πε02pr3

Caution Direction is along p (from −q to +q). The short-dipole field falls as 1/r3, not 1/r2.

DerivationField on the equatorial line of a dipole

Obtain the field at a point on the equatorial line of a dipole. (B23 Q9)

P on the perpendicular bisector at OP = r; AP = BP = √(r2 + l2).

  1. Magnitudes are equal: E+ = E− = kq/(r2+l2).
  2. E+ points away from +q, E− towards −q: the components perpendicular to the axis cancel.
  3. Components parallel to the axis add, each E+ cos θ, with cos θ = l/√(r2+l2).
  4. E = 2E+ cos θ = 2kql/(r2+l2)3/2.
Eeq = 14πε0p(r2 + l2)3/2, antiparallel to p   ⇒   short dipole: E = 14πε0pr3

Caution At the same large distance Eaxial = 2Eeq. Drawing both component arrows pointing away from the axis is the classic wrong figure.

DerivationTorque on a dipole in a uniform field

Show that the torque on a dipole in a uniform field is p × E. (S27 Q9(ii))

Dipole at angle θ to a uniform field E.

  1. Force qE on +q along E, and qE on −q against it: net force zero.
  2. The two equal, opposite, non-collinear forces form a couple. Their lines of action are parallel to E, so the arm is the perpendicular distance between them, 2l sin θ.
  3. τ = force × arm = qE × 2l sin θ = pE sin θ.
τ = p × E,   τ = pE sin θ

Caution Maximum pE at 90°; zero at 0° (stable) and 180° (unstable). The torque turns p towards E.

DerivationPotential energy of a dipole in a uniform field

Work done by an external agent turning the dipole slowly from θ1 to θ2 against the torque pE sin θ.

  1. dW = τ dθ = pE sin θ dθ.
  2. W = ∫ pE sin θ dθ from θ1 to θ2 = pE(cos θ1 − cos θ2).
  3. Choose the zero of energy at θ1 = 90°: U(θ) = −pE cos θ.
U = −p·E = −pE cos θ

Caution 0°: −pE (stable, minimum); 90°: 0; 180°: +pE (unstable). Work to turn from 0° to 180° is 2pE.

DerivationPotential due to a point charge

Derive V = Q/4πε0r. (S26 Q9 — due on a board paper)

Bring a unit positive test charge from infinity to P at distance r from +Q.

  1. At distance x the field pushes outwards with E = kQ/x2; the agent pulls inwards through dx, doing dW = −E dx.
  2. V = −∫∞r kQ/x2 dx = kQ [1/x]∞r.
  3. Hence the work per unit charge is kQ/r; between two points VA − VB = kQ(1/rA − 1/rB).
V = 14πε0Qr

Caution V is a scalar: positive for +Q, negative for −Q. It falls as 1/r while E falls as 1/r2.

DerivationPotential on the axis of a dipole

P on the axis, OP = r; distances r−l from +q and r+l from −q.

  1. V = kq/(r−l) − kq/(r+l) (scalars, simply added).
  2. = kq·2l/(r2−l2).
Vaxial = 14πε0pr2 − l2 ⇒ short dipole kp/r2;   Vequatorial = 0

Caution At a general point of a short dipole V = kp cos θ/r2, which gives both results.

DerivationGauss: infinitely long line charge

Line with charge λ per metre. By symmetry E is radial and has the same size at the same r.

  1. Gaussian surface: a coaxial cylinder of radius r, length l.
  2. Flat ends: E lies along them, flux 0. Curved face: E normal and constant, flux E(2πrl).
  3. Charge enclosed λl. Gauss: E·2πrl = λl/ε0.
E = λ2πε0r = 2kλr   (radially outward for λ > 0)

Caution Falls as 1/r. Doubling λ and halving r makes the field four times larger (B24 Q2(ii)).

DerivationGauss: infinite plane sheet

Sheet with surface density σ. E is normal to the sheet, equal and opposite on the two sides.

  1. Gaussian surface: a cylinder (pill box) of end area A crossing the sheet.
  2. Curved face: E parallel to it, flux 0. Two ends: EA each, total 2EA.
  3. Charge enclosed σA: 2EA = σA/ε0.
E = σ2ε0   independent of distance

Caution Two parallel sheets +σ and −σ: fields add between them (σ/ε0) and cancel outside. A charged conductor has σ/ε0 just outside because the field inside it is zero.

DerivationGauss: thin spherical shell (inside, on, outside)

Shell of radius R with charge Q. By symmetry E is radial and depends only on r.

  1. Outside (r > R): concentric Gaussian sphere of radius r; flux E·4πr2 = Q/ε0, so E = kQ/r2 — as if all the charge were at the centre.
  2. On the surface (r = R): E = kQ/R2 = σ/ε0.
  3. Inside (r < R): the Gaussian sphere encloses no charge, so E = 0.
E = 0 (r < R),   kQ/R2 (r = R),   kQ/r2 (r > R)

Caution The potential is not zero inside: it is constant, equal to kQ/R. The syllabus names the E–r graph; draw it.

DerivationCapacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor, with and without a slab

Plates of area A, separation d, charges ±Q, σ = Q/A.

  1. Between the plates the two sheet fields add: E0 = σ/ε0 = Q/ε0A.
  2. Air gap only: V = E0d = Qd/ε0A, so C = Q/V = ε0A/d.
  3. With a slab of thickness t: in the slab the field is E0/K; in the remaining air E0.
  4. V = E0(d − t) + (E0/K)t = (Q/ε0A)(d − t + t/K).
C = ε0Ad   →   C′ = ε0Ad − t + t/K

Caution Check the limits: t = 0 gives ε0A/d; t = d gives Kε0A/d. A metal slab (K = ∞) gives ε0A/(d−t).

DerivationCapacitors in series and in parallel

Three capacitors C1, C2, C3 across a supply V.

  1. Series: the same charge q sits on each (charge cannot cross the gaps); the voltages add: V = q/C1 + q/C2 + q/C3.
  2. Dividing by q and writing V/q = 1/Cs gives the series rule.
  3. Parallel: the same V across each; the charges add: q = C1V + C2V + C3V.
  4. Dividing by V gives Cp.
1Cs = 1C1 + 1C2 + 1C3    Cp = C1 + C2 + C3

Caution n identical capacitors: Cs = C/n, Cp = nC, so Cs/Cp = 1/n2 (three give 1/9).

Worked exampleA thundercloud as a parallel-plate capacitor (S27 Q2(i))

ES-1

The base of a thundercloud of area 4·5 × 108 m2 is 4425 m above flat ground. Treating cloud and ground as a parallel-plate capacitor, find its capacitance.

Show working
  1. Air between the "plates", so C = ε0A/d.
  2. C = 8·85 × 10−12 × 4·5 × 108 / 4425 = 9·0 × 10−7 F.

Answer C = 9·0 × 10−7 F (about 0·9 μF).

Worked exampleA charged body held up by a sheet (S27 Q2(ii))

ES-2

A small body of mass 0·05 kg carrying charge 8 × 10−17 C floats at rest above a large horizontal sheet of charge. Find the surface charge density of the sheet (g = 9·8 m s−2).

Show working
  1. Field of an infinite sheet: E = σ/2ε0, upward.
  2. Equilibrium: qE = mg, so σ = 2ε0mg/q.
  3. σ = 2 × 8·85 × 10−12 × 0·05 × 9·8 / (8 × 10−17) = 1·08 × 105 C m−2.

Answer σ = 1·08 × 105 C m−2. (Unit C m−2 — CISCE’s own key misprints it as V m−1.)

Worked exampleFlux through one face by symmetry (competency C68)

ES-3

A charge 2 × 10−6 C sits 5 cm above the centre of a square of side 10 cm. Find the flux through the square.

Show working
  1. The square is one face of a cube of side 10 cm with the charge at its centre.
  2. Total flux through the cube q/ε0; the six faces are equivalent, so each gets q/6ε0.
  3. φ = 2 × 10−6 / (6 × 8·85 × 10−12) = 37700 N m2 C−1.

Answer φ = 37700 N m2 C−1.

Worked examplePotential energy of three charges (S23 Q2(ii))

ES-4

Three charges of 5 × 10−8 C each sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 3 m. Find the work needed to assemble them from infinity.

Show working
  1. Three pairs, each at distance a: U = 3kq2/a.
  2. U = 3 × 9 × 109 × (5 × 10−8)2 / 3 = 2·25 × 10−5 J.

Answer W = U = 2·25 × 10−5 J.

Worked exampleAxial and equatorial field of a dipole

ES-5

Charges ±10−6 C are 0·02 m apart. Find the field at 0·2 m from the centre (a) on the axis, (b) on the equatorial line. Compare (a) with the short-dipole value.

Show working
  1. p = q(2l) = 2·00 × 10−8 C m; l = 0·01 m.
  2. (a) E = 2kpr/(r2−l2)2 = 2 × 9 × 109 × 2 × 10−8 × 0·2 / (0·0399)2 = 45200 N C−1, along p.
  3. (b) E = kp/(r2+l2)3/2 = 180 / (0·0401)3/2 = 22400 N C−1, opposite to p.
  4. Short-dipole value 2kp/r3 = 45000 N C−1: within 0·5 %, since r = 20l.

Answer 45200 N C−1 on the axis; 22400 N C−1 on the equator (about half).

Worked exampleCapacitor half filled with a dielectric (S25 Q2(i))

ES-6

An air capacitor has C0 = 12 pF. A slab of dielectric constant 3 and thickness half the gap is slid in. Find the new capacitance. If the battery stays connected, by what factor does the charge change?

Show working
  1. C′ = ε0A/(d−t+t/K) with t = d/2: C′ = C0/(½ + 1/6) = 1·5 C0.
  2. C′ = 1·80 × 10−11 F = 18 pF.
  3. Battery connected: V fixed, so Q ∝ C: charge rises by a factor 1·5.

Answer C′ = 18 pF; charge × 1·5.

Worked exampleCharge and energy in a network (B19 Q14 type)

ES-7

3 μF and 6 μF are in series; the pair is in parallel with 4 μF, across 12 V. Find the equivalent capacitance, the charge drawn and the energy stored.

Show working
  1. Series pair: 3 × 6/(3 + 6) = 2·0 × 10−6 F (2 μF).
  2. Add 4 μF in parallel: C = 6·0 × 10−6 F (6 μF).
  3. Q = CV = 7·2 × 10−5 C (72 μC).
  4. U = ½CV2 = ½ × 6 × 10−6 × 144 = 4·32 × 10−4 J.

Answer 6 μF, 72 μC, 4·32 × 10−4 J.

Worked exampleField of one sheet and of two sheets (B25 Q9, S23 1A(i))

ES-8

A large thin sheet carries 1·77 × 10−5 C m−2. Find the field near it. A second sheet with −σ is placed parallel to it: find the field between them and outside.

Show working
  1. One sheet: E = σ/2ε0 = 17·7 × 10−6/(2 × 8·85 × 10−12) = 1·0 × 106 N C−1, away from the sheet.
  2. Between +σ and −σ the two fields point the same way: E = σ/ε0 = 2·0 × 106 N C−1, from + to −.
  3. Outside they are opposite and equal: E = 0.

Answer 1·0 × 106 N C−1; 2·0 × 106 N C−1 between; 0 outside.

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Drawing the equatorial-field components both pointing away from the axis (that is two like charges). E− points towards −q.
  • Using the horizontal gap 2l cos θ as the arm of the dipole couple; the arm is perpendicular to the forces.
  • Counting charges instead of pairs in the PE of a system: 3 charges → 3 terms, 4 charges → 6 terms.
  • Saying V = 0 inside a charged shell. E is zero; V is constant and equal to its surface value.
  • Forgetting which quantity is fixed when a dielectric goes in (Q if disconnected, V if connected).
  • Using σ/ε0 for an isolated thin sheet (it is σ/2ε0).
  • Flux through a surface with charges outside: they contribute nothing to the net flux, though they do change E on the surface.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Q9 derivation (3 marks): axial field (S27, B26 — highest) or equatorial field; OR torque on a dipole τ = p × E.
  • Due from specimens: potential of a point charge (S26 Q9), Gauss for the shell with the E–r graph (S25 Q9), dipole moment of a molecule (S25/S26 Q3).
  • Gauss flux one-markers (charges inside/outside, radius doubled), capacitor combinations and dielectric effects, parallel-plate capacitance in a real-world context (S27 Q2 style).
  • Equipotential ordering and work done along an equipotential (A–R or MCQ in 1(A)).

2. Current Electricity

Unit 2 · with Electrostatics 14 marks · drift, Ohm, cells, Kirchhoff, bridges, potentiometer

ConceptDrift, mobility and Ohm’s law

  • Free electrons move randomly at ~105 m s−1; a field adds a tiny drift velocity vd (~mm s−1) opposite to E.
  • Relaxation time τ: mean time between collisions. Mobility μ = vd/E = eτ/m (m2 V−1 s−1).
  • Ohm’s law: V = IR at constant temperature; micro-form J = σE. R = ρl/A; ρ depends on material and temperature only, not on V.
  • Non-ohmic: filament lamp (curve bends as it heats), diode, electrolyte. Current doubled in a wire: vd doubles, τ unchanged.
  • Temperature: metals ρ = ρ0(1 + αΔT), τ falls as T rises; semiconductors: n rises steeply, so ρ falls.

vd = eEτ/m: the field sets it, the collisions limit it.

ConceptCells: emf, internal resistance, combinations

  • emf ε = work done per unit charge by the source; terminal p.d. V = ε − Ir on discharge, ε + Ir while charging. V–I graph: intercept ε, slope −r.
  • n identical cells in series: nε, nr. In parallel: ε, r/n. Mixed, m rows of n: I = nε/(R + nr/m), maximum when R = nr/m.
  • Two unequal cells in parallel: εeq = (ε1r2 + ε2r1)/(r1 + r2), req = r1r2/(r1+r2).
  • Power P = VI = I2R = V2/R; 1 kWh = 3·6 × 106 J ("unit" on the bill). Bulbs in series: the lower-wattage one (larger R) glows brighter.

ConceptKirchhoff, bridges and the potentiometer

  • Junction law ΣI = 0: conservation of charge. Loop law ΣΔV = 0: conservation of energy. Going with the current through R: −IR; through a cell from − to +: +ε.
  • Wheatstone bridge balanced (Ig = 0): P/Q = R/S. Swapping battery and galvanometer leaves the balance unchanged. Metre bridge: R/S = l/(100 − l).
  • Potentiometer principle: a steady current in a uniform wire makes V ∝ l: V = kl, k the potential gradient (V m−1). At balance no current is drawn, so it measures the true emf — an ideal voltmeter.
  • Sensitivity improves with a longer wire / smaller k. The driver emf must exceed the emf being measured, and the + terminals must be joined at the same end.
  • NCERT (rationalised) dropped the potentiometer and metre bridge; ISC 2027 keeps both.

Balance means zero current in the galvanometer, not zero current anywhere else.

DerivationCurrent and drift velocity: I = nAevd

Wire of cross-section A, n free electrons per m3, each drifting at vd.

  1. In time t every electron within a length vdt crosses a section: number nAvdt.
  2. Charge crossing q = nAvdt·e; I = q/t.
I = nAevd,   J = I/A = nevd

Caution For a wire of varying cross-section, I is the same everywhere, so vd ∝ 1/A (larger in the narrow part).

Derivationvd = eEτ/m, and hence σ = ne2τ/m

An electron between collisions accelerates in the field E: a = eE/m (opposite to E).

  1. Just after a collision its velocity is random with average zero. After time t it has gained at.
  2. Averaging over all electrons, the mean time since the last collision is τ: vd = aτ = eEτ/m.
  3. Put this in J = nevd: J = (ne2τ/m)E.
  4. Compare with J = σE (Ohm’s law): the bracket is the conductivity.
vd = eEτm,   σ = ne2τm,   ρ = mne2τ

Caution This also proves Ohm’s law: at fixed T, n and τ are fixed, so J ∝ E, i.e. I ∝ V.

DerivationTerminal voltage from energy: V = ε − Ir

A cell of emf ε and internal resistance r drives I through R.

  1. In time dt charge dq = I dt passes; the cell does work dW = εdq = εI dt.
  2. This appears as heat in R and r: εI dt = I2R dt + I2r dt.
  3. So ε = I(R + r) and the p.d. across the terminals is V = IR.
I = εR + r,   V = ε − Ir

Caution On open circuit (I = 0) V = ε; short-circuit current ε/r.

DerivationCombination of cells: series, parallel, mixed, and two unequal cells

Identical cells (ε, r) feeding an external R.

  1. Series (n): the emfs add and so do the internal resistances, I = nε/(R + nr).
  2. Parallel (m): same emf; m equal resistances in parallel give r/m, I = ε/(R + r/m).
  3. Mixed: each row is (nε, nr), and m rows in parallel give (nε, nr/m).
  4. Unequal pair in parallel: terminal p.d. V is common; I1 = (ε1−V)/r1, I2 = (ε2−V)/r2; I = I1+I2 rearranges to V = εeq−Ireq.
I = nεR + nr/m ;   εeq = ε1r2 + ε2r1r1 + r2, req = r1r2r1 + r2

Caution Series is best when R >> r; parallel when R << r.

DerivationBalance condition of a Wheatstone bridge (take Ig = 0)

At balance no current flows through G, so B and D are at the same potential.

  1. The current I1 in P continues unchanged through Q; I2 in R continues through S.
  2. Same potential at B and D: the drops from A are equal, I1P = I2R.
  3. Likewise from B and D to C: I1Q = I2S.
  4. Divide the two equations.
PQ = RS

Caution The syllabus says Kirchhoff is not needed: start from Ig = 0. Metre bridge: the wire segments of length l and 100 − l are the other two arms, so R/S = l/(100 − l).

DerivationPotentiometer: comparing emfs and finding internal resistance

Driver cell ε0 keeps a steady current in the uniform wire AB, so the fall of potential along it is V = kl.

  1. Close ε1 into the circuit; the jockey balances at l1: no current in the cell, so ε1 = kl1.
  2. Switch to ε2: balance at l2, ε2 = kl2. Divide: ε1/ε2 = l1/l2.
  3. Internal resistance (second figure): with the key open balance at l1 gives ε = kl1. Close it through R: the cell now delivers current and its terminal p.d. V = kl2 balances.
  4. V = IR and ε = I(R + r), so r = R(ε/V − 1).
ε1ε2 = l1l2 ,    r = R(l1l2 − 1)

Caution No balance anywhere on the wire? Either the driver emf is too small or the + terminals are not joined at the same end (C57 asks you to spot exactly this).

Worked exampleDrift speed in a copper-like wire (B20 Q2(a))

CE-1

A wire of cross-section 1 mm2 carries 5 A. Free-electron density 2 × 1028 m−3. Find the drift speed.

Show working
  1. vd = I/nAe = 5/(2 × 1028 × 10−6 × 1·6 × 10−19) = 1·56 × 10−3 m s−1.

Answer vd = 1·56 × 10−3 m s−1 ≈ 1·56 mm s−1.

Worked exampleTwo-loop Kirchhoff network (B20 Q15, S26 Q10(ii) type)

CE-2

In the network below, find the current in each branch and the p.d. between X and Y. Cells have negligible internal resistance.

Left branch 10 V with 2 Ω; middle 4 Ω; right 4 V with 2 Ω.

Show working
  1. Junction X: I1 + I3 = I2 (I1, I3 up the outer branches, I2 down the middle).
  2. Loop left + middle: 10 = 2I1 + 4I2. Loop right + middle: 4 = 2I3 + 4I2.
  3. Subtract: I1 − I3 = 3. With the junction law, 10 = 2I1 + 4(2I1 − 3) gives I1 = 2·2 A.
  4. I3 = −0·80 A (negative: 0·8 A flows down the right branch, charging the 4 V cell), I2 = 1·4 A.
  5. VXY = 4I2 = 5·6 V.

Answer I1 = 2·2 A, I2 = 1·4 A, 0·8 A into the 4 V cell; VXY = 5·6 V.

Worked examplePotential gradient and an unknown emf (B24 Q10(ii))

CE-3

A driver cell of emf 6 V and internal resistance 2 Ω is joined through 20 Ω to a potentiometer wire 10 m long of resistance 28 Ω. A cell balances at 4·5 m. Find the current, the potential gradient and the emf.

Show working
  1. I = 6/(2 + 28 + 20) = 0·12 A.
  2. k = IRwire/L = 0·12 × 28/10 = 0·336 V m−1.
  3. ε = kl = 0·336 × 4·5 = 1·51 V.

Answer 0·12 A; 0·336 V m−1; ε = 1·51 V.

Worked exampleInternal resistance by potentiometer (S24/S25 Q4(ii))

CE-4

A cell balances at 110 cm on open circuit and at 100 cm when shunted by 10 Ω. Find its internal resistance.

Show working
  1. r = R(l1/l2 − 1) = 10(110/100 − 1) = 1·0 Ω.

Answer r = 1·0 Ω.

Worked exampleMetre bridge with a parallel pair (S27 Q10(ii))

CE-5

In a metre bridge the right gap holds 12 Ω in parallel with 24 Ω. The null point is 60 cm from the left end. Find the resistance R1 in the left gap.

Show working
  1. Right gap: 12 × 24/36 = 8·0 Ω.
  2. R1/8 = 60/40, so R1 = 12 Ω.

Answer R1 = 12 Ω.

Worked exampleMixed grouping of cells (B23 Q10(i) type)

CE-6

6 rows, each of 8 cells in series, are joined in parallel. Each cell has emf 2 V and internal resistance 0·5 Ω. Find the current in an external 6 Ω and the terminal p.d.

Show working
  1. Each row: 16 V and 4 Ω; six rows in parallel: emf 16 V, internal resistance 0·667 Ω.
  2. I = 16/(6 + 0·667) = 2·4 A.
  3. V = IR = 14·4 V.

Answer I = 2·4 A, V = 14·4 V.

Worked exampleTwo unequal cells in parallel (B26 Q10(ii) type)

CE-7

Cells (2 V, 1 Ω) and (4 V, 3 Ω) are joined in parallel, + to +, across 4·25 Ω. Find the equivalent emf and internal resistance and the current in R.

Show working
  1. εeq = (2 × 3 + 4 × 1)/(1 + 3) = 2·5 V.
  2. req = 1 × 3/4 = 0·75 Ω.
  3. I = 2·5/(4·25 + 0·75) = 0·50 A.

Answer 2·5 V, 0·75 Ω, 0·5 A.

Worked exampleRated bulb on a lower supply

CE-8

A bulb is rated 220 V, 100 W. Find its resistance, and the power it takes on 110 V (resistance assumed constant).

Show working
  1. R = V2/P = 2202/100 = 484 Ω.
  2. P = 1102/484 = 25 W — a quarter, since P ∝ V2.

Answer 484 Ω; 25 W.

Worked exampleTemperature coefficient of resistance (NCERT type)

CE-9

A coil has resistance 2·1 Ω at 27 °C and 2·7 Ω at 100 °C. Find α.

Show working
  1. α = (R2−R1)/[R1(T2−T1)] = 0·6/(2·1 × 73) = 3·91 × 10−3 °C−1.

Answer α = 3·91 × 10−3 °C−1.

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Dividing by the wrong length in the metre bridge: the resistance in the left gap goes with the length measured from the left end.
  • Forgetting the driver cell’s internal resistance and the series resistor when finding the potentiometer current.
  • Treating a negative Kirchhoff current as an error: it only means the assumed direction was wrong.
  • Writing r = R(l2/l1 − 1): the open-circuit (longer) length goes on top.
  • Saying drift velocity changes the relaxation time; τ depends only on the material and temperature.
  • Brightness in series: the lower rated wattage is brighter (larger R, same I).

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Q10 numerical with OR (3 marks, 8 boards out of 8): a two-loop Kirchhoff network OR a potentiometer with a driver cell (current, gradient, unknown emf).
  • Labelled potentiometer circuit to compare emfs or find r (S27 Q3, B26 Q4(ii)); spot-the-error in a potentiometer circuit (C57).
  • Balanced metre bridge / Wheatstone with a combination in one arm (S27 Q10(ii)); cell combinations (S27 Q10(i)).
  • Drift velocity: numerical, or what happens to vd and τ when V, l or T change.
  • Derivations due: I = nAevd, σ = ne2τ/m, and the Wheatstone condition (syllabus "derive").

3. Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism

Unit 3 · with EMI and AC 16 marks · Biot–Savart, Ampère, forces, torque, galvanometer, magnetic materials

ConceptSources of B: Biot–Savart and Ampère

  • Oersted: a current deflects a compass. Biot–Savart: dB = (μ0/4π) I dl sin θ/r2; vector form dB = (μ0/4π) I dl × r/r3.
  • Ampère: ∮B·dl = μ0Ienc. Long wire B = μ0I/2πr; long solenoid B = μ0nI inside (uniform), ~0 outside; at an end half of that.
  • Finite straight wire (formula only): B = (μ0I/4πd)(sin α + sin β).
  • Direction: right-hand thumb rule (Ampère’s swimming rule is not in the syllabus). B lines always form closed loops — there are no magnetic monopoles.

A current loop is a magnetic dipole, m = NIA, pointing along the thumb when the fingers curl with I.

ConceptForces: Lorentz, conductors, parallel wires

  • F = q(E + v × B). The magnetic part is perpendicular to v, so it does no work: speed and kinetic energy are unchanged.
  • v ⊥ B: circle, r = mv/qB, f = qB/2πm (independent of speed). At an angle: helix. v ∥ B: no force.
  • Crossed fields: undeviated when qE = qvB, v = E/B — for any charge and mass (a velocity selector).
  • Conductor: F = I l × B. Parallel wires: F/l = μ0I1I2/2πr; like currents attract, unlike repel.
  • One ampere: the current which, in two long parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum, produces a force of 2 × 10−7 N per metre. Then 1 C = 1 A s.

ConceptTorque, magnetic moment and the moving-coil galvanometer

  • Rectangular coil in uniform B: τ = m × B, τ = NIAB sin φ with φ between the normal and B. Net force zero.
  • Revolving electron (Bohr orbit): I = ev/2πr, so μ = IA = evr/2 = (e/2m)L.
  • MCG: concave pole pieces + soft-iron core give a radial field, so the plane of the coil is always along B and τ = NIAB; balanced by the spring kφ: I = (k/NAB)φ, a linear scale.
  • Current sensitivity φ/I = NAB/k; voltage sensitivity φ/V = NAB/kG. Doubling N doubles current sensitivity but (doubling G too) leaves voltage sensitivity unchanged.
  • Ammeter: small shunt in parallel, S = IgG/(I−Ig). Voltmeter: large resistance in series, R = V/Ig − G. Ideal ammeter 0 Ω, ideal voltmeter ∞.

ConceptMagnetism and matter

  • Diamagnetic (Bi, Cu, water, N2): χ small negative, μr < 1, weakly repelled, field lines thinned, independent of T; a rod sets perpendicular to B.
  • Paramagnetic (Al, Pt, Na, O2): χ small positive, μr slightly > 1, weakly attracted; Curie law χ ∝ 1/T; rod sets parallel.
  • Ferromagnetic (Fe, Co, Ni, Gd): χ very large, μr >> 1, domains; above the Curie temperature (Fe 770 °C) becomes paramagnetic. μr = 1 + χ; H = B/μ0 − M.
  • B–H loop (qualitative): soft iron — low coercivity, narrow loop, small hysteresis loss: electromagnets and transformer cores. Steel — high retentivity and high coercivity: permanent magnets.
  • Bar magnet ~ a solenoid: field lines leave N and enter S outside, run S → N inside. Field on the axial and equatorial lines is qualitative only (no derivation, no numericals); torque τ = m × B.
  • Electromagnet strength rises with N, I and the core’s μr.

Odd one out: Fe, Ni, Co are ferro; Pt (and Al) are para (S27 1A(ii)).

DerivationB at the centre of a circular coil (Biot–Savart)

Coil of radius R, N turns, current I.

  1. Every element dl is at distance R from the centre and perpendicular to the radius, so sin θ = 1.
  2. dB = (μ0/4π) I dl/R2, and every element gives dB in the same direction (along the axis).
  3. Add them: Σdl = 2πR per turn, so B = (μ0/4π) I(2πR)/R2 per turn.
B = μ0NI2R

Caution Scaling: doubling I, N and R together doubles B. Rewinding the same wire into a coil of radius 2R halves N, so B falls to a quarter.

DerivationB at a point on the axis of a circular coil

Point P on the axis at distance x from the centre; each element is at r = √(R2 + x2) from P, and dl ⊥ r.

  1. dB = (μ0/4π) I dl/r2, perpendicular to r, so it makes angle θ with the axis-normal plane.
  2. Resolve: dB cos θ perpendicular to the axis — cancels with the element diametrically opposite; dB sin θ along the axis — adds.
  3. sin θ = R/r: B = Σ(μ0/4π) I dl R/r3 = (μ0/4π) I (2πR) R/r3.
B = μ0NIR22(R2 + x2)3/2   along the axis

Caution Checks: x = 0 gives μ0NI/2R; x = R gives B0/2√2; x = 2R gives B0/5√5. For x >> R, B = μ02m/4πx3 — a dipole field.

DerivationB near a long straight wire (Ampère)

Long straight wire with current I. By symmetry B has the same size everywhere on a circle centred on the wire and is tangent to it.

  1. Amperian loop: circle of radius r concentric with the wire.
  2. B ∥ dl at every point, so ∮B·dl = B(2πr).
  3. Current enclosed I: B(2πr) = μ0I.
B = μ0I2πr

Caution Statement first: "the line integral of B round any closed loop equals μ0 times the current threaded through it". The same method with a rectangular loop gives μ0nI inside a solenoid (qualitative in the syllabus).

DerivationForce between two parallel currents; the ampere

Wires A and B, distance r apart, currents I and I′ in the same direction.

  1. A’s field at B: BA = μ0I/2πr, perpendicular to B.
  2. Force on a length l of B: F = I′lBA (l ⊥ B), directed towards A by the right-hand rule.
  3. By Newton’s third law A is pulled towards B equally.
Fl = μ0II′2πr ;   attract if parallel, repel if antiparallel

Caution Putting I = I′ = 1 A, r = 1 m gives 2 × 10−7 N m−1: the definition of the ampere. A third wire is in equilibrium where the two fields cancel, I1/r1 = I2/r2.

DerivationTorque on a current loop in a uniform field

Rectangular coil, sides l (⊥ to the paper) and b, N turns, in uniform B; the normal makes angle φ with B.

  1. The two sides of length b feel equal and opposite forces along the same line: they cancel.
  2. The two sides of length l feel F = NIlB each, opposite, a couple.
  3. The perpendicular distance between their lines of action is b sin φ: τ = NIlB·b sin φ = NIAB sin φ.
τ = m × B,   τ = NIAB sin φ,   m = NIA

Caution Measure φ from the normal, not from the plane: from the plane the same figure gives cos. Torque is zero when the plane is perpendicular to B, maximum when B lies in the plane.

DerivationCharged particle in a uniform magnetic field

Charge q, mass m, entering with v ⊥ B.

  1. The force qvB is perpendicular to v: it changes the direction, never the speed. A constant-size force always perpendicular to the velocity gives uniform circular motion.
  2. It supplies the centripetal force: qvB = mv2/r.
  3. Period T = 2πr/v.
r = mvqB = √2mKqB,   T = 2πmqB,   f = qB2πm

Caution The period does not depend on speed. With a component of v along B the path is a helix of pitch v cos θ·T.

DerivationConverting a galvanometer into an ammeter and a voltmeter

Galvanometer of resistance G giving full-scale deflection at Ig.

  1. Ammeter of range I: a shunt S in parallel must carry I−Ig. Same p.d.: IgG = (I−Ig)S.
  2. The ammeter’s resistance GS/(G+S) is less than S.
  3. Voltmeter of range V: a resistance R in series; at full scale Ig(G + R) = V.
S = IgGI − Ig ,    R = VIg − G

Caution Ammeter in series (low R), voltmeter in parallel (high R). This is also practical experiment 1 (convert to 2 A and to 4 V).

DiagramMagnetic materials at a glance

FormulaeMagnetism formula sheet

QuantityFormulaNote
Biot–SavartdB = (μ0/4π)I dl sin θ/r2μ0 = 4π × 10−7 T m A−1
Coil centre / axisμ0NI/2R,   μ0NIR2/2(R2+x2)3/2
Wire / solenoidμ0I/2πr,   μ0nIn turns per metre
LorentzF = q(E + v × B)velocity selector v = E/B
Circular motionr = mv/qB, f = qB/2πm
Conductor, wiresF = BIl sin θ,   F/l = μ0I1I2/2πr
Torqueτ = NIAB sin φ, m = NIAφ from the normal
GalvanometerI = (k/NAB)φ; S = IgG/(I−Ig); R = V/Ig−G

Worked exampleForce per metre between two wires (S23 Q5(i))

MG-1

Two long parallel wires 0·05 m apart carry 5 A and 10 A in opposite directions. Find the force per metre and its nature.

Show working
  1. F/l = μ0I1I2/2πr = 2 × 10−7 × 50/0·05 = 2·0 × 10−4 N m−1.
  2. Opposite currents: repulsive.

Answer 2·0 × 10−4 N m−1, repulsive.

Worked exampleRadius of an electron’s path (S23 Q5(ii))

MG-2

An electron enters a field 3 × 10−3 T at right angles with speed 8 × 106 m s−1. Find the radius of its path.

Show working
  1. r = mv/eB = 9·1 × 10−31 × 8 × 106/(1·6 × 10−19 × 3 × 10−3) = 0·0152 m.

Answer r ≈ 1·5 cm.

Worked exampleFrequency of revolution of a proton (B25 Q12(ii))

MG-3

Find the frequency of revolution of a proton in 0·314 T (mp = 1·67 × 10−27 kg).

Show working
  1. f = eB/2πm = 1·6 × 10−19 × 0·314/(2π × 1·67 × 10−27) = 4·79 × 106 Hz.
  2. Independent of the speed.

Answer f ≈ 4·8 MHz.

Worked exampleShunt and series resistance (B23 Q5(ii), H16 Q6(b))

MG-4

(a) A galvanometer of resistance 55 Ω reads full scale at 0·25 A. What shunt converts it to a 0–3 A ammeter? (b) One of 50 Ω and 0·01 A is to read 0–20 V: what series resistance?

Show working
  1. (a) S = IgG/(I−Ig) = 0·25 × 55/2·75 = 5·0 Ω, in parallel.
  2. (b) R = V/Ig − G = 20/0·01 − 50 = 1950 Ω, in series.

Answer 5 Ω shunt; 1950 Ω in series.

Worked exampleTorque on a square coil (NCERT 4.9)

MG-5

A square coil of 20 turns and side 0·1 m carries 12 A in a field 0·8 T; its normal makes 30 ° with the field. Find the torque.

Show working
  1. τ = NIAB sin φ = 20 × 12 × 0·01 × 0·8 × 0·5 = 0·96 N m.

Answer 0·96 N m.

Worked exampleField near a long wire (NCERT 4.3, competency C53)

MG-6

A long horizontal wire carries 50 A from north to south. Find the field 2·5 m east of it and its direction.

Show working
  1. B = μ0I/2πr = 2 × 10−7 × 50/2·5 = 4·0 × 10−6 T.
  2. Right-hand rule, thumb south: to the east of the wire the field points vertically upward.

Answer 4·0 × 10−6 T, upward.

Worked exampleField at the centre and on the axis of a coil (S26 Q12(i))

MG-7

A coil of 100 turns, radius 0·08 m, carries 0·4 A. Find B at the centre and at a point on the axis a distance R from the centre.

Show working
  1. B0 = μ0NI/2R = 4π × 10−7 × 100 × 0·4/0·16 = 3·14 × 10−4 T.
  2. At x = R: B = μ0NIR2/2(2R2)3/2 = B0/2√2 = 1·11 × 10−4 T.

Answer 3·14 × 10−4 T and 1·11 × 10−4 T.

Worked exampleCrossed fields (S27 Q11)

MG-8

An electric field 30000 V m−1 and a magnetic field 0·02 T are perpendicular to each other and to a beam of α-particles, which passes undeviated. Find the speed. What happens if the α-particles are replaced by protons of the same speed?

Show working
  1. Undeviated: qE = qvB, v = E/B = 1·5 × 106 m s−1.
  2. The condition does not contain q or m: protons at the same speed also pass undeviated.

Answer 1·5 × 106 m s−1; protons are also undeviated.

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Measuring the torque angle from the plane of the coil instead of the normal.
  • Circulation arrows inconsistent with the stated current direction in the coil and Ampère figures.
  • Rewinding a wire into a larger coil: N changes too (same length of wire), so B ∝ 1/R2, not 1/R.
  • Saying a magnetic field changes the kinetic energy of a charge. It cannot: F ⊥ v.
  • Voltage sensitivity rises with N: false if the extra turns also raise G proportionally.
  • Calling platinum or aluminium ferromagnetic; putting soft iron in a permanent magnet.
  • Using a bar-magnet end-on / broadside field formula: out of the 2027 syllabus (qualitative only).

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Q11 derivation (3 marks, every paper): B at the centre of a coil (B24, B26) or B near a long wire by Ampère (B23, S26), or the axis field with the B0/2√2 check (S25/S26 — due).
  • Force between parallel wires, the ampere, and a floating third wire in equilibrium (B26 Q12).
  • Galvanometer: conversion numerical, radial field, current vs voltage sensitivity (B26 Q11(ii), S26 Q5).
  • Charged particle in B (radius, frequency) and crossed fields (S27 Q11).
  • One-markers: odd one out among materials, χ against T, soft iron vs steel, field-scaling of coils and solenoids.

4. Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents

Unit 4 · with Magnetism 16 marks; Q18 (5 marks) is always this unit · Faraday, Lenz, inductance, transformer, ac circuits, generator

ConceptFaraday, Lenz and motional emf

  • Flux φ = B·A = BA cos θ (weber). Faraday: ε = −N dφ/dt; the emf lasts only while the flux changes.
  • Lenz: the induced current opposes the change that causes it — a statement of energy conservation (you must do work against it). Direction: Fleming’s right-hand rule for a moving rod.
  • Motional emf: a rod of length l moving at v across B gets ε = Blv; with the circuit closed through R, power P = (Blv)2/R. Rotating rod: ε = ½Bωl2.
  • Eddy currents: loops of induced current in bulk metal; they heat cores and damp motion. Reduced by laminating (thin insulated sheets). Uses: electromagnetic braking, induction furnace, damping a galvanometer.
  • Blue spark at a switch: breaking the circuit makes dI/dt huge, so the self-induced emf L dI/dt is large enough to ionise the air gap (S27 Q5).

Induced emf needs a changing flux; a steady field and a stationary loop give nothing.

ConceptSelf and mutual inductance, transformer

  • Self: φ = LI, ε = −L dI/dt; 1 H = 1 V s A−1. Solenoid L = μ0N2A/l (× μr with a core). Energy ½LI2.
  • Mutual: φ2 = MI1, ε2 = −M dI1/dt. Coaxial solenoids M = μ0n1N2A.
  • Transformer (mutual induction, ac only): Vs/Vp = Ns/Np = Ip/Is (ideal). Step-up at the power station, step-down in the city and in a phone charger.
  • Losses: copper (I2R; thick wire), eddy (laminated core), hysteresis (soft iron), flux leakage (windings on top of each other). Power is transmitted at high voltage so that I and the I2R loss in the lines are small.

ConceptAC circuits and power

  • v = V0 sin ωt; Vrms = V0/√2 (mains 220 V rms, 311 V peak); mean over half a cycle 2V0/π, over a full cycle 0.
  • Pure R: in phase. Pure L: V leads I by π/2, XL = ωL (grows with f). Pure C: I leads by π/2, XC = 1/ωC (falls with f; blocks dc).
  • Series LCR: Z = √[R2 + (XL−XC)2], tan φ = (XL−XC)/R. Resonance XL = XC: f0 = 1/2π√(LC), Z = R minimum, current maximum; VL and VC are equal and opposite and can each exceed the supply.
  • Power P = VrmsIrms cos φ = Irms2R; power factor cos φ = R/Z. Pure L or C: cos φ = 0, wattless current. A choke coil limits ac current with almost no power loss.
  • Sharpness: smaller R gives a taller, sharper resonance peak (larger Q; no derivation). LC oscillations: energy swaps between C and L at ω0 = 1/√(LC) (qualitative).
  • AC generator: coil rotating at ω in B gives ε = NBAω sin ωt. AC is preferred because it can be stepped up and down by transformers.

In a capacitor the current leads (ICE); in an inductor the voltage leads (ELI).

DerivationMotional emf, and the power needed to keep the rod moving

Rod PQ of length l slides at v on rails closed by R; B is perpendicular to the plane.

  1. In time dt the rod sweeps area lv dt: dφ = Blv dt.
  2. Faraday: |ε| = dφ/dt = Blv. (Equivalently, the Lorentz force evB on each electron over length l.)
  3. Current I = Blv/R; the field pushes back on the rod with F = BIl = B2l2v/R (Lenz).
  4. To keep v constant an agent must supply P = Fv.
ε = Blv,   P = (Blv)2R = I2R

Caution The mechanical power equals the heat in R: energy is conserved, which is Lenz’s law in numbers. If x is given as a function of t, differentiate for v first (S27 Q18(i)(b)).

DerivationSelf-inductance of a long solenoid, and mutual inductance of two coaxial solenoids

Solenoid of length l, N turns, cross-section A, current I; n = N/l.

  1. Field inside B = μ0nI, uniform over A.
  2. Flux linked with all N turns: Nφ = N(μ0nI)A = μ0N2AI/l.
  3. Compare with Nφ = LI for L.
  4. Second coil of N2 turns wound on the first (same A): flux linkage N2(μ0n1I1)A = MI1.
L = μ0N2Al = μ0n2Al,    M = μ0N1N2Al

Caution Same number of turns rewound into half the length and half the radius: N unchanged, A/4, l/2, so L halves. (If the same length of wire is rewound at half the radius, N doubles and L = μ0N2A/l doubles instead — read which is held fixed.) With a core multiply by μr.

DerivationRMS and mean values of a sinusoidal current

I = I0 sin ωt, period T = 2π/ω.
  1. Mean-square: ⟨I2⟩ = (1/T)∫0T I02 sin2ωt dt.
  2. sin2ωt = ½(1 − cos 2ωt), and cos 2ωt averages to zero over a cycle: ⟨I2⟩ = I02/2.
  3. RMS is the dc current giving the same heating: Irms = √⟨I2⟩.
  4. Mean over a half cycle: (2/T)∫0T/2 I0 sin ωt dt = (2I0/ωT)[−cos ωt]0T/2 = 2I0/π.
Irms = I0√2 = 0·707 I0,   Imean (half cycle) = 2I0π = 0·637 I0

Caution The mean over a full cycle is zero, which is why ac meters read rms. Meter readings, "220 V mains" and ratings are all rms.

DerivationAC through pure R, pure L and pure C (phasors)

Apply v = V0 sin ωt to each element alone (Kirchhoff’s loop law).

  1. R: V0 sin ωt = iR ⇒ i = (V0/R) sin ωt: in phase.
  2. L: V0 sin ωt = L di/dt ⇒ i = −(V0/ωL) cos ωt = I0 sin(ωt − π/2): current lags by π/2, XL = ωL.
  3. C: q = CV0 sin ωt ⇒ i = dq/dt = ωCV0 cos ωt = I0 sin(ωt + π/2): current leads by π/2, XC = 1/ωC.
XL = ωL = 2πfL,   XC = 1ωC = 12πfC

Caution Average power in pure L or C over a cycle is zero: sin × cos averages to zero.

DerivationImpedance and phase of a series LCR circuit

The same current i = I0 sin ωt flows through R, L and C in series. Take the current phasor as reference.

  1. VR = I0R in phase with I; VL = I0XL ahead by 90°; VC = I0XC behind by 90°.
  2. VL and VC are opposite: their resultant is VL−VC, perpendicular to VR.
  3. Phasor sum: V02 = VR2 + (VL−VC)2 = I02[R2 + (XL−XC)2].
  4. The angle between V0 and I: tan φ = (VL−VC)/VR.
Z = √R2 + (XL − XC)2,   tan φ = XL − XCR,   i = (V0/Z) sin(ωt − φ)

Caution RL circuit: drop XC; RC: drop XL (φ negative, current leads). Add the peak (or rms) voltages as phasors, never arithmetically.

DerivationResonance and average power

Vary the frequency with R, L, C and V0 fixed.

  1. Z is least when XL = XC: ω0L = 1/ω0C.
  2. Then Z = R, φ = 0, the current is V0/R (maximum) and the power factor is 1.
  3. Average power: p = V0 sin ωt·I0 sin(ωt−φ); the average of sin ωt sin(ωt−φ) over a cycle is ½ cos φ.
f0 = 12π√LC,   Pav = ½V0I0 cos φ = VrmsIrms cos φ = Irms2R,   cos φ = R/Z

Caution Keeping f0 fixed when C is doubled needs L halved (S24 Q18(ii)(b)). Below f0 the circuit is capacitive, above it inductive.

DerivationAC generator: e = NBAω sin ωt

Coil of N turns and area A rotates at ω in uniform B; at t = 0 its normal is along B.

  1. Angle between normal and field at time t: θ = ωt.
  2. Flux linkage Nφ = NBA cos ωt.
  3. ε = −d(Nφ)/dt = NBAω sin ωt.
ε = ε0 sin ωt,   ε0 = NBAω

Caution The emf is maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to B (flux zero, but changing fastest), zero when perpendicular. Slip rings give ac; a split-ring commutator would give dc.

DerivationTransformer ratios (ideal)

Same flux φ through every turn of both coils (no leakage), no losses.

  1. Primary: back emf Npdφ/dt balances Vp. Secondary: Vs = Nsdφ/dt.
  2. Divide: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.
  3. No losses: VpIp = VsIs.
VsVp = NsNp = IpIs,   efficiency η = Pout/Pin

Caution A transformer does not work on dc (no changing flux). Step-up raises V and lowers I; the winding with more current is the one with fewer turns (thicker wire).

TransformerVs/Vp = Ns/Np = Ip/Isideal

Worked exampleMotional emf when x is a function of time (S27 Q18(i)(b))

EA-1

A metal axle 1·2 m long moves along level tracks so that its displacement is x = (3t2 + 6) m. The vertical component of the earth’s field is 2 × 10−5 T. Find the emf across the axle at t = 10 s.

Show working
  1. v = dx/dt = 6t = 60 m s−1 at 10 s.
  2. ε = Blv = 2 × 10−5 × 1·2 × 60 = 1·44 × 10−3 V.

Answer ε = 1·44 × 10−3 V = 1·44 mV.

Worked exampleCurrent, retarding force and power (S23 Q18(ii))

EA-2

A rod 0·8 m long slides at 36 km h−1 (10 m s−1) on rails in a field 0·2 T perpendicular to the rails; the circuit resistance is 5 Ω. Find the emf, the current, the force needed to keep the speed and the power delivered.

Show working
  1. ε = Blv = 0·2 × 0·8 × 10 = 1·6 V.
  2. I = ε/R = 0·32 A.
  3. F = BIl = 0·2 × 0·32 × 0·8 = 0·0512 N.
  4. P = Fv = 0·512 W = ε2/R.

Answer 1·6 V, 0·32 A, 0·0512 N, 0·512 W.

Worked exampleSelf-inductance from a falling current (B24 Q18(ii)(a))

EA-3

A current of 5 A falls to zero in 0·02 s and induces 500 V in the coil. Find L and the energy that was stored.

Show working
  1. L = ε/(dI/dt) = 500/(5/0·02) = 2·0 H.
  2. U = ½LI2 = ½ × 2 × 25 = 25 J.

Answer L = 2 H, 25 J.

Worked exampleInductance of a solenoid and of a coaxial pair

EA-4

A solenoid of 500 turns is 0·5 m long with cross-section 10−3 m2. A second coil of 100 turns is wound over its middle. Find L of the solenoid and M of the pair.

Show working
  1. L = μ0N2A/l = 4π × 10−7 × 2·5 × 105 × 10−3/0·5 = 6·28 × 10−4 H.
  2. M = μ0N1N2A/l = 1·26 × 10−4 H.

Answer L = 6·28 × 10−4 H, M = 1·26 × 10−4 H.

Worked examplePeak and rms current, period, power (S27 Q18(ii))

EA-5

A voltage v = 300 sin 100πt volt is applied across 100 Ω. Find the peak and rms current, the frequency and period, and the average power. Sketch one cycle of the current.

Show working
  1. I0 = V0/R = 3·0 A; Irms = 3/√2 = 2·12 A.
  2. ω = 100π: f = 50 Hz, T = 0·020 s.
  3. P = ½V0I0 = ½ × 300 × 3 = 450 W.
  4. Graph: a sine of amplitude 3 A crossing zero at 0, 0·01 and 0·02 s.

Answer 3 A, 2·12 A, 50 Hz, 0·02 s, 450 W.

Worked exampleIdentify the element from a graph (S27 Q18(i)(a))

EA-6

A graph shows e = 240 sin ωt and a current of peak 6 A that reaches its maximum a quarter-period before the voltage; the period is 80 ms. Identify the element and find its reactance and value.

Show working
  1. Current leads by π/2: a pure capacitor.
  2. f = 1/T = 12·5 Hz.
  3. XC = V0/I0 = 40 Ω.
  4. C = 1/(2πfXC) = 1/(2π × 12·5 × 40) = 3·18 × 10−4 F.

Answer Capacitor; 12·5 Hz; 40 Ω; 3·18 × 10−4 F.

Worked exampleSeries LCR: Z, current, phase, power, resonance (B18 Q20(b))

EA-7

A 100 Ω resistor, a 1 H inductor and a 16 μF capacitor are in series with v = 300 sin 100πt. Find XL, XC, Z, the peak current, the phase angle, the average power and the resonant frequency.

Show working
  1. XL = 100π × 1 = 314·2 Ω; XC = 1/(100π × 16 × 10−6) = 198·9 Ω.
  2. Z = √(1002 + 115·22) = 152·6 Ω.
  3. I0 = 300/152·6 = 1·97 A.
  4. tan φ = 115·2/100: φ = 49·0 °, voltage leads (inductive); cos φ = 0·655.
  5. P = Irms2R = (1·966)2/2 × 100 = 193 W.
  6. f0 = 1/2π√(1 × 16 × 10−6) = 39·8 Hz.

Answer Z ≈ 153 Ω, I0 ≈ 1·97 A, φ ≈ 49°, P ≈ 193 W, f0 ≈ 39·8 Hz.

Worked exampleA choke coil on the mains (B25I Q18(i))

EA-8

A coil of inductance 0·5 H and resistance 50 Ω is connected to 220 V, 50 Hz. Find the current, the phase lag and the power factor.

Show working
  1. XL = 2π × 50 × 0·5 = 157·1 Ω; Z = √(502 + 157·12) = 164·8 Ω.
  2. Irms = 220/164·9 = 1·33 A.
  3. tan φ = 157·1/50: φ = 72·3 ° (current lags); cos φ = R/Z = 0·303.

Answer 1·33 A, lagging by 72·3°, power factor 0·303.

Worked exampleInductance from dc and ac readings (B26 Q18(i)(a))

EA-9

A coil takes 1 A from a 200 V dc supply and 0·5 A from 200 V, 50 Hz ac. Find its inductance.

Show working
  1. dc: only resistance, R = 200/1 = 200 Ω.
  2. ac: Z = 200/0·5 = 400 Ω; XL = √(4002 − 2002) = 346·4 Ω.
  3. L = XL/2πf = 1·10 H.

Answer L ≈ 1·10 H.

Worked exampleResonance: current and the voltage across L (S23 Q18(i))

EA-10

A series circuit of 80 Ω, 1 H and 40 μF is fed by a variable-frequency 220 V (rms) source. Find the resonant frequency, the current at resonance, the reactances and the rms voltage across L.

Show working
  1. f0 = 1/2π√(40 × 10−6) = 25·2 Hz.
  2. Z = R: I = 220/80 = 2·75 A.
  3. XL = XC = 2πf0L = 158·1 Ω.
  4. VL = IXL = 2·75 × 158·1 = 435 V — about twice the supply, cancelled by an equal VC.

Answer 25·2 Hz; 2·75 A; 158 Ω; VL ≈ 435 V.

Worked exampleStep-up transformer (B23 Q18(ii)(b))

EA-11

An ideal transformer has 60 primary and 3000 secondary turns. The primary is on 220 V and carries 5 A. Find the secondary voltage and current.

Show working
  1. Vs = 220 × 3000/60 = 11000 V.
  2. Is = VpIp/Vs = 1100/11000 = 0·10 A.

Answer 11 kV; 0·1 A.

Worked examplePeak emf of a generator (competency C44)

EA-12

A square coil of 20 turns and side 0·08 m rotates at 50 rev s−1 in a field 0·03 T. Find the peak emf and the average emf over a full cycle.

Show working
  1. ε0 = NBAω = 20 × 0·03 × 0·0064 × 2π × 50 = 1·21 V.
  2. Over a full cycle the emf is positive for half and negative for half: average 0.

Answer 1·21 V; zero.

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Adding VR, VL and VC arithmetically to get the supply voltage.
  • Saying a capacitor lags: in C the current leads the voltage by 90°.
  • Using f where ω is needed: 100π rad s−1 is 50 Hz.
  • Forgetting to differentiate x(t) for the speed in a motional-emf question.
  • Believing a transformer steps up power; it steps up voltage and steps down current.
  • Maximum generator emf when the coil’s plane is perpendicular to B: it is when the plane is parallel.
  • Taking rms as peak for mains: 220 V is rms, the peak is 311 V.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Q18 (5 marks, every board): series LCR / RL numerical (Z, I, φ, power factor, power) OR identify the element from a graph, plus self-inductance from ε = L dI/dt, transformer turns and currents, rms from e = e0 sin ωt.
  • Motional emf with v from x(t) (S27), rails with current, force and power.
  • L from dc and ac readings (B26), resonance frequency and VL at resonance, current vs frequency for different R (S25/S26).
  • Blue spark / eddy currents / laminated core (S27 Q5), Lenz direction for a coil approaching a loop (S27 Q12(ii)).
  • Derivations to hold: rms value, LCR impedance by phasors, f0, generator emf, L of a solenoid.

5. Electromagnetic Waves

Unit 5 · 2 marks, always Section B · displacement current, properties, the spectrum

ConceptDisplacement current and the nature of EM waves

  • Between the plates of a charging capacitor no charge flows, yet Ampère’s law must still hold. Maxwell added the displacement current id = ε0 dφE/dt, equal to the conduction current in the leads: a changing electric field produces a magnetic field.
  • An accelerated charge radiates. The wave has E and B in phase, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel (E × B): transverse.
  • Speed in vacuum c = 1/√(μ0ε0) = 3 × 108 m s−1 for every band; E0 = cB0. No medium is needed; they carry energy and momentum.
  • In a medium v = c/n; frequency is set by the source and does not change on refraction.

X-rays, red light and radio waves share the same speed in vacuum and are all transverse (NCERT 8.3, B26 Q7(ii)).

DerivationDisplacement current equals the conduction current

A parallel-plate capacitor of plate area A is being charged by a current i.

  1. Charge on the plates q; field between them E = q/ε0A; flux φE = EA = q/ε0.
  2. id = ε0dφE/dt = dq/dt = i.
id = ε0dφEdt = ic ;   ∮B·dl = μ0(ic + id)

Caution Syllabus: "basic idea" only. The current is continuous through the gap, as conduction current outside and displacement current inside.

DiagramThe electromagnetic spectrum

Worked exampleFrequency from wavelength and naming the band (B25 Q7(ii))

EW-1

Find the frequency of radiation of wavelength 6 nm and name the band. Which band has wavelength 10 m?

Show working
  1. f = c/λ = 3 × 108/6 × 10−9 = 5·0 × 1016 Hz: soft X-rays. The bands overlap here (NCERT: X-rays from about 10 nm down, UV down to about 0·6 nm), so “far ultraviolet” is also accepted; B25 asked only for the frequency.
  2. 10 m: f = 3·0 × 107 Hz = 30 MHz, radio (short-wave).

Answer 5·0 × 1016 Hz, soft X-rays (or far UV); 10 m is radio.

Worked exampleElectric amplitude from magnetic amplitude (NCERT 8.6)

EW-2

The magnetic field of a plane EM wave has amplitude 510 nT. Find the amplitude of the electric field.

Show working
  1. E0 = cB0 = 3 × 108 × 5·1 × 10−7 = 153 V m−1.

Answer 153 V m−1.

Worked exampleThe speed of light from μ0 and ε0

EW-3

Using μ0 = 4π × 10−7 T m A−1 and ε0 = 8·85 × 10−12 F m−1, find c.

Show working
  1. c = 1/√(4π × 10−7 × 8·85 × 10−12) = 3·00 × 108 m s−1.

Answer 3·00 × 108 m s−1 — Maxwell’s evidence that light is an EM wave.

Worked exampleRate of change of field in a charging capacitor (NCERT 8.1)

EW-4

Circular plates of radius 0·12 m are charged by a current of 0·15 A. Find the displacement current and the rate of change of the field between the plates.

Show working
  1. id = ic = 0·15 A.
  2. dE/dt = i/(ε0πr2) = 0·15/(8·85 × 10−12 × π × 0·0144) = 3·75 × 1011 V m−1 s−1.

Answer 0·15 A; 3·75 × 1011 V m−1 s−1.

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Saying EM waves need a medium, or that different bands travel at different speeds in vacuum.
  • Mixing the order of IR and UV, or of X-rays and gamma rays (gamma has the highest frequency).
  • Naming "radio" for radar: radar uses microwaves. TV remote and fog photography: infrared.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Q7 (2 marks, 14 of 14 papers): name the EM wave from a use or an image (luggage scanner, satellite dish, TV remote, haze photography, radar) plus one property or source.
  • Arrange the bands by increasing frequency or wavelength (S27 Q6); one common property (transverse, same speed).
  • Displacement current: its basic idea in one line.

6. Optics (i): Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

Unit 6(i) · Optics 18 marks, about 11–13 from ray optics · mirrors, refraction, TIR, lenses, prism, instruments

ConceptMirrors and the sign convention

  • New Cartesian convention: distances from the pole, positive in the direction of the incident light, heights positive upward. Real images of a concave mirror have negative v.
  • Mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, R = 2f, magnification m = −v/u.
  • Concave: object beyond C → real, inverted, diminished; between F and P → virtual, erect, magnified (shaving mirror). Convex: always virtual, erect, diminished (rear-view mirror, wide field).
  • A mirror’s focal length does not depend on the surrounding medium (reflection involves no n): a convex mirror in water keeps the same f (S27 1A(vii)).

ConceptRefraction, total internal reflection and fibres

  • Snell: n1 sin i = n2 sin r; n = c/v; 1n2 × 2n3 × 3n1 = 1. Frequency is unchanged; λ and speed fall by n.
  • Real and apparent depth: n = real depth / apparent depth (viewed near-normally).
  • TIR: light going from denser to rarer, angle of incidence greater than the critical angle, sin C = 1/n. Diamond sparkles (C ≈ 24°); mirage.
  • Total reflecting prisms (45°–45°–90°, n > √2): turn a ray through 90° or 180° (periscope, binoculars), or invert an image.
  • Optical fibre: core of higher n in cladding of lower n; light entering within the acceptance cone is totally reflected along it. Uses: endoscopy, telecommunication.

TIR needs both: denser → rarer, and i > C.

ConceptLenses, power and combinations

  • Lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, m = v/u. Lens maker: 1/f = (n−1)(1/R1 − 1/R2).
  • In a liquid use the relative index ng/nl: the focal length grows; if the liquid’s n equals the glass’s the lens vanishes (acts as a plane sheet); if it is larger, a convex lens diverges.
  • Power P = 1/f (f in metres, dioptre). In contact: P = P1 + P2.
  • Cut lenses: halved along the axis (horizontally), each half has the same f and forms the same image with half the brightness. Cut perpendicular to the axis (plano-convex halves), each half has 2f.
  • Lens and mirror combination: take the image of each element as the object for the next; an image coinciding with the object means the rays hit the mirror normally.

ConceptPrism, dispersion, rainbow

  • A = r1 + r2, δ = i + e − A. At minimum deviation i = e, r1 = r2 = A/2 and the ray inside is parallel to the base.
  • The i–δ curve falls to a single minimum and rises: any other δ is produced by two values of i.
  • Thin prism: δ = (n − 1)A. Violet deviates most (largest n). Angular dispersion δv − δr; dispersive power ω = (nv−nr)/(ny−1) = (δv−δr)/δy. A larger δ does not mean a larger ω.
  • Rainbow (no derivation): refraction and dispersion on entering the drop, one total internal reflection, refraction on leaving; primary bow red outside at about 42°, violet inside at 40°. The secondary has two internal reflections and reversed colours.

ConceptOptical instruments

  • Simple microscope (object inside F): M = 1 + D/f with the image at D = 25 cm, D/f with the image at infinity; shorter f, larger M.
  • Compound microscope: objective (short f, small aperture) forms a real magnified image inside the eyepiece’s focus. M = (vo/uo)(1 + D/fe) at D; ≈ (L/fo)(D/fe) at infinity.
  • Astronomical telescope, normal adjustment: M = fo/fe, tube length fo + fe; image at D: M = (fo/fe)(1 + fe/D). Objective: long focus and large aperture (brighter, better resolution).
  • Reflecting telescope (Cassegrain): a concave paraboloidal primary mirror and a convex secondary. No chromatic aberration, no spherical aberration with a paraboloid, a large mirror is easier to support than a large lens, brighter image. Hubble is in orbit to avoid atmospheric absorption and twinkling.

DerivationMirror formula (concave mirror, real image)

Object AB on the axis of a concave mirror of focus F; image A′B′. Small aperture: the mirror’s surface is taken as the plane through P.

  1. Ray through the pole: triangles ABP and A′B′P are similar, so A′B′/AB = PB′/PB.
  2. Ray parallel to the axis, reflected through F: triangles (mirror point M, P, F) and A′B′F are similar, so A′B′/MP = B′F/FP; and MP = AB, so A′B′/AB = B′F/FP.
  3. Equate: PB′/PB = (PB′ − PF)/PF. With the sign convention PB = −u, PB′ = −v, PF = −f: v/u = (v−f)/f.
  4. Cross-multiply and divide by uvf.
1v + 1u = 1f,   m = −vu,   f = R/2

Caution R = 2f: a ray parallel to the axis at height h meets the mirror at angle θ to the normal CM; reflection makes the triangle CMF isosceles, so CF = FM ≈ FP for small apertures, hence PF = PC/2.

DerivationRefraction at a single spherical surface

Point object O in the rarer medium (n1), convex surface of radius R (centre C) into the denser medium (n2); real image I. Paraxial rays.

  1. Snell at N: n1 sin i = n2 sin r ⇒ n1i = n2r (small angles).
  2. Exterior angles: i = α + γ (triangle ONC), γ = r + β (triangle NCI), so r = γ − β.
  3. With NM the perpendicular from N to the axis and P the pole (M ≈ P for paraxial rays): α ≈ NM/PO, β ≈ NM/PI, γ ≈ NM/PC.
  4. Substitute: n1(1/PO + 1/PC) = n2(1/PC − 1/PI). Signs: PO = −u, PI = +v, PC = +R.
n2v − n1u = n2 − n1R

Caution The syllabus fixes the case: convex towards the rarer medium, real image. The figure is not to scale; the angles are opened out so they can be labelled.

DerivationLens maker’s formula and the thin-lens formula

Thin lens of index n in air, surfaces of radii R1 and R2; object O at u.

  1. First surface alone (air → glass) would form I′ at v′: n/v′ − 1/u = (n−1)/R1.
  2. I′ is the object for the second surface (glass → air), which forms I at v: 1/v − n/v′ = (1 − n)/R2 (thin lens: distances from the same point).
  3. Add: the n/v′ terms cancel, giving 1/v − 1/u = (n−1)(1/R1 − 1/R2).
  4. For an object at infinity the image is at F: v = f.
1f = (n − 1)(1R1 − 1R2) ,    1v − 1u = 1f

Caution Biconvex: R1 > 0, R2 < 0. Equiconvex with n = 1·5 has f = R. In a liquid replace (n − 1) by (ng/nl − 1).

DerivationTwo thin lenses in contact

Lenses of focal lengths f1 and f2 in contact; object O at u.

  1. The first lens alone forms I1 at v1: 1/v1 − 1/u = 1/f1.
  2. I1 is a (virtual) object for the second lens at the same distance v1 (no separation): 1/v − 1/v1 = 1/f2.
  3. Add the two equations.
1F = 1f1 + 1f2,   P = P1 + P2

Caution Magnification of a combination = product of the magnifications. A concave lens of the same power in contact gives a plane sheet (P = 0).

DerivationRefraction through a prism: n = sin[(A + δm)/2] / sin(A/2)

A ray enters a prism of angle A at M and leaves at N; incidence i, refraction r1, r2, emergence e.

  1. In the quadrilateral formed by the two faces and the two normals, the angle between the normals is 180° − A; in the triangle with the ray inside, r1 + r2 + (180° − A) = 180°, so A = r1 + r2.
  2. Deviation at the two faces: (i−r1) + (e−r2), so δ = i + e − A.
  3. At minimum deviation the path is symmetric: i = e, r1 = r2 = r. Then r = A/2 and i = (A + δm)/2.
  4. Snell at the first face: n = sin i/sin r.
n = sin [(A + δm)/2]sin (A/2)

Caution Thin prism (small A): sin x ≈ x gives δ = (n − 1)A. For an equilateral prism at δm the ray inside is parallel to the base.

DerivationMagnifying power of a simple microscope

Object of height h; unaided, the best view is at the near point D, subtending θ0 = h/D.

  1. Image at D: v = −D. Lens formula gives u: 1/u = −1/D − 1/f.
  2. Angle subtended by the image (eye close to the lens) = angle of the object at the lens, θ = h/|u|.
  3. M = θ/θ0 = D/|u| = 1 + D/f.
  4. Image at infinity: the object is at F, θ = h/f, M = D/f.
M = 1 + Df (image at D),   M = Df (image at ∞)

Caution MP increases as f decreases (S27 Q15(ii)). "Normal use" of a magnifier means the image is at D.

DerivationMagnifying power of a compound microscope (image at D)

Objective (fo) and eyepiece (fe); final image at D.

  1. Objective: real, inverted, magnified image, mo = vo/uo.
  2. Eyepiece used as a simple microscope with the image at D: me = 1 + D/fe.
  3. Total: M = mome.
M = vo|uo|(1 + Dfe) ;   image at ∞: M ≈ Lfo · Dfe

Caution Both lenses have short focal lengths, the objective the shorter. Length of the tube at D: vo + |ue|.

DerivationMagnifying power of an astronomical telescope

Distant object subtending α at the objective (fo); eyepiece fe.

  1. The objective forms a real, inverted image of height h at its focus: α ≈ h/fo.
  2. Normal adjustment: this image is also at the eyepiece’s focus, so the final image is at infinity, subtending β = h/fe.
  3. M = β/α.
  4. Image at D instead: the eyepiece forms it at D, ue from 1/ue = −1/D − 1/fe, and β = h/|ue|.
M = fofe, L = fo + fe   (normal);   M = fofe(1 + feD) at D

Caution The final image is inverted (no matter for stars). A long-focus, large-aperture objective and a short-focus eyepiece.

DiagramTIR, the fibre and the rainbow
