Worked exampleRefractive index from minimum deviation (S27 Q14(i))

RO-1

A prism of angle 60 ° gives a minimum deviation of 34 °. Find its refractive index.

Show working
  1. n = sin[(60° + 34°)/2]/sin 30° = sin 47°/0·5 = 1·46.

Answer n = 1·46 (sin 47° = 0·7314; CISCE’s key rounds this to 1·47).

Worked exampleThe same prism in water (NCERT 9.6, B26 Q13)

RO-2

An equilateral glass prism (60 °) has minimum deviation 40 ° in air. Find n, and the minimum deviation when it is immersed in water (1·33).

Show working
  1. ng = sin 50°/sin 30° = 1·532.
  2. In water the relative index is 1·152.
  3. sin[(60° + δm)/2] = 1·152 × 0·5 = 0·576; (60° + δm)/2 = 35·2°.
  4. δm = 10·3 °.

Answer n = 1·53; in water δm ≈ 10·3°.

Worked exampleLens maker, in air and in water (B18 Q7)

RO-3

A biconvex lens (n = 1·5) has radii 20 cm and 30 cm. Find its focal length in air and in water (1·33).

Show working
  1. Signs: R1 = +20 cm, R2 = −30 cm.
  2. 1/f = 0·5(1/20 + 1/30) = 0·5 × 5/60: f = 24·0 cm.
  3. In water: 1/f′ = (1·5/1·33 − 1)(1/12) = 0·1278/12: f′ = 93·9 cm.

Answer 24 cm in air; about 94 cm in water — the power falls to about a quarter.

Worked exampleImage by a single refracting surface (S27 Q20(ii))

RO-4

A point object in air is 60 cm in front of a convex spherical surface of radius 20 cm bounding glass of index 1·5. Locate the image.

Show working
  1. n2/v − n1/u = (n2−n1)/R with u = −60 cm, R = +20 cm.
  2. 1·5/v = 0·5/20 − 1/60 = 1/120, so v = 180 cm.

Answer v = +180 cm: a real image inside the glass.

Worked examplePower of a combination (B25 Q6)

RO-5

Lenses of power +2·0 D and −1·5 D are in contact. Find the focal length and nature of the combination.

Show working
  1. P = 2·0 − 1·5 = 0·50 D.
  2. F = 1/P = 2·0 m, positive: converging.

Answer 2 m, converging.

Worked exampleConcave mirror with the object inside F (B23 1A(iv))

RO-6

An object is 10 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Find the image position, magnification and nature.

Show working
  1. Signs: u = −10 cm, f = −20 cm.
  2. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/20 + 1/10 = 1/20: v = 20 cm.
  3. m = −v/u = 2·0.

Answer Virtual, erect, twice the size, 20 cm behind the mirror.

Worked exampleCompound microscope, image at D (B20 Q17(a) = B25I Q13, recycled)

RO-7

A compound microscope has fo = 1·5 cm and fe = 5 cm. An object is 1·6 cm from the objective and the final image is at 25 cm. Find the magnifying power and the separation of the lenses.

Show working
  1. Objective: 1/vo = 1/1·5 − 1/1·6: vo = 24·0 cm.
  2. Eyepiece, image at 25 cm: |ue| = 1/(1/25 + 1/5) = 4·17 cm.
  3. M = (24/1·6)(1 + 25/5) = 15 × 6 = 90.
  4. Separation = 24 + 4·17 = 28·2 cm.

Answer M = 90; the lenses are 28·2 cm apart.

Worked exampleAstronomical telescope (NCERT 9.11)

RO-8

A telescope has an objective of focal length 144 cm and an eyepiece of 6 cm. Find the magnifying power and tube length in normal adjustment, and the magnifying power with the final image at 25 cm.

Show working
  1. Normal: M = 144/6 = 24, L = 150 cm.
  2. At D: M = 24(1 + 6/25) = 29·76.

Answer 24, 150 cm; 29·76.

Worked exampleArea of water surface through which light escapes (NCERT 9.5)

RO-9

A small bulb is 0·8 m below the surface of water (1·33). Find the area of the surface through which light emerges.

Show working
  1. Light escapes only where it meets the surface at less than the critical angle: sin C = 1/1·33, C = 48·75 °.
  2. Radius of the circle r = h tan C = 0·8 × tan 48·75° = 0·912 m.
  3. Area πr2 = 2·61 m2.

Answer About 2·6 m2.

Worked exampleDispersive power from deviations (B19 Q8)

RO-10

A thin prism deviates violet, yellow and red light by 3·75 °, 3·25 ° and 2·86 °. Find the angular dispersion and the dispersive power.

Show working
  1. Angular dispersion δv − δr = 0·89 °.
  2. ω = 0·89/3·25 = 0·274.

Answer 0·89°; ω = 0·274 (no unit).

Worked exampleMagnifying glass (S22b Q3(i))

RO-11

Find the magnifying power of a convex lens of focal length 5 cm used as a simple microscope with the image (a) at 25 cm, (b) at infinity. Where is the object in (a)?

Show working
  1. (a) M = 1 + 25/5 = 6·0; object at 1/(1/25 + 1/5) = 4·17 cm from the lens.
  2. (b) M = 25/5 = 5·0.

Answer 6 and 5; the object is 4·17 cm from the lens.

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Dropping the sign convention half-way; write u, v, f, R with signs before substituting.
  • Marking r1 and r2 along the ray instead of from the normals in the prism figure.
  • Using the absolute index of glass for a lens in a liquid; it is ng/nl.
  • Saying a larger δm means a larger dispersive power.
  • Telescope ray diagram with the intermediate image not at the common focus in normal adjustment, or with arrows missing.
  • Reflecting telescope advantage "higher magnification": the real advantages are no chromatic aberration, larger aperture, brighter image.
  • Changing frequency on refraction: only speed and wavelength change.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Prism (every board but one): derive n = sin[(A + δm)/2]/sin(A/2) with the i–δ graph, or a numerical (n from δm, grazing emergence, liquid on a face).
  • Instrument ray diagram: compound microscope with image at D (S24–S26 Q16) or telescope at infinity (B26 Q14), with MP; the reflecting telescope’s advantages.
  • Derivations due: lens maker (S23, S26 — not yet on a board), single spherical surface, lenses in contact.
  • One-markers: lens in a liquid / convex mirror in water (A–R), lens combination power, cut lens (S27 Q15(i)), frequency unchanged on refraction.
  • Numericals recycled with the same data: B20 → B25I microscope (1·5 cm, 5 cm, 1·6 cm).

6. Optics (ii): Wave Optics

Unit 6(ii) · about 5–7 of the 18 optics marks · wavefronts, Huygens, interference, single-slit diffraction

ConceptWavefronts and Huygens’ principle

  • A wavefront is the locus of points vibrating in the same phase; rays are normal to it. The phase difference between two points on one wavefront is zero.
  • Point source: spherical; line source (slit): cylindrical; very distant source: plane.
  • Huygens: every point of a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets travelling at the wave speed; the new wavefront is the forward envelope (common tangent) of the wavelets after time t.
  • Syllabus limits: proof of reflection and refraction only; Huygens for a prism or lens is excluded.

ConceptInterference

  • Coherent sources have a constant phase difference (and the same frequency); two independent lamps are not coherent because their phases change randomly every ~10−8 s. YDSE makes two coherent sources by dividing one wavefront.
  • Path difference Δx and phase difference φ = (2π/λ)Δx. Bright: Δx = nλ (φ = 2nπ); dark: (n + ½)λ.
  • Sustained interference needs coherent sources, nearly equal amplitudes, narrow slits close together, and monochromatic light.
  • Fringe width β = λD/d: grows with λ and D, shrinks with d; blue fringes are narrower than red; in a liquid β/n. White light: central white fringe, coloured fringes either side. Covering one slit: the fringes vanish, leaving single-slit diffraction.
  • Intensity I ∝ (amplitude)2: Imax/Imin = (a1+a2)2/(a1−a2)2. Energy is redistributed, not destroyed.

Interference fringes are equally spaced and equally bright; diffraction has a broad bright centre and weaker, narrower sides.

ConceptSingle-slit diffraction

  • Minima at a sin θn = nλ (n = 1, 2, …); secondary maxima near a sin θ = (n + ½)λ.
  • Central maximum: angular width 2λ/a, linear width 2λD/a; twice as wide as the others and much brighter. Narrower slit or longer wavelength: wider pattern.
  • Noticeable diffraction needs an aperture or obstacle comparable with λ (B25 1A(vii)).
  • The pattern proves the wave nature of light; so does interference.

DerivationLaw of reflection by Huygens’ principle

Plane wavefront OB falls obliquely on a reflecting surface; O touches the surface first, and B reaches the surface at O′ a time t later. Speed c.

  1. In time t the far end travels BO′ = ct, while the wavelet from O spreads to a hemisphere of radius OC = ct (same medium, same speed).
  2. The reflected wavefront is the tangent O′C drawn from O′ to that wavelet.
  3. Right-angled triangles OBO′ and O′CO (right angles at B and C): hypotenuse OO′ common, BO′ = OC. So they are congruent (RHS).
  4. Hence ∠BOO′ = ∠CO′O. These are the angles the incident and reflected wavefronts make with the surface, which equal i and r.
i = r , and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane

Caution The two equal sides are BO′ and OC, not the two wavefronts OB and O′C. Name RHS: that is where the marks are.

DerivationSnell’s law by Huygens’ principle

Plane wavefront OB meets the boundary between a rarer medium (speed c1) and a denser one (c2 < c1); O is on the boundary.

  1. In time t the point B travels BO′ = c1t in the first medium; the wavelet from O spreads only OC = c2t into the second.
  2. The refracted wavefront is the tangent O′C from O′ to the wavelet centred at O.
  3. On the common hypotenuse OO′: sin i = BO′/OO′, sin r = OC/OO′ (the wavefronts make angles i and r with the boundary).
  4. Divide: OO′ and t cancel.
sin isin r = c1c2 = 1n2 = constant

Caution Draw both the incident and the refracted wavefronts and mark i and r (B25 Q14). The frequency is fixed by the source; speed and wavelength fall.

DerivationYoung’s double slit: fringe width

Slits A and B, separation d, screen at distance D (D >> d); point P at height y above the centre O.

  1. Drop the perpendicular AN on BP: the path difference is BN = d sin θ.
  2. Small angles: sin θ ≈ tan θ = y/D, so Δx = yd/D.
  3. Bright fringe: yd/D = nλ ⇒ yn = nλD/d. Dark fringe: yn = (n + ½)λD/d.
  4. Fringe width: distance between consecutive bright (or dark) fringes, yn+1 − yn.
β = λDd

Caution The mathematical deduction of intensity from two wave equations is not required, but the intensity graph is.

DerivationSingle slit: position of minima and width of the central maximum

Slit of width a, plane wave of wavelength λ, screen at D.

  1. Divide the slit into two halves. For direction θ the path difference between the edges is a sin θ.
  2. If a sin θ = λ, each point in the upper half has a partner in the lower half λ/2 out of step: they cancel in pairs — the first minimum.
  3. Generally a sin θn = nλ gives minima; between them, at (n+½)λ, one uncancelled third survives: weak secondary maxima.
  4. Central maximum between the first minima on either side: angular half-width λ/a.
a sin θn = nλ (minima),   angular width 2λ/a,   linear width 2λD/a

Caution Everything scales as λ/a: halve the slit and the central maximum doubles in width.

FormulaeWave optics formula sheet

QuantityFormulaNote
Phase and pathφ = (2π/λ)Δx
YDSEΔx = d sin θ = yd/D, β = λD/dbright nλ, dark (n+½)λ
In a liquidβ′ = β/n
IntensitiesImax/Imin = (a1+a2)2/(a1−a2)2I ∝ a2
Single slita sin θ = nλ, width 2λD/a

Worked exampleFringe width, positions and a change of colour (B20 Q17(b) = B25 Q16, recycled)

WO-1

In a YDSE d = 5 mm, D = 1·2 m and λ = 600 nm. Find (a) β, (b) the distance of the 10th bright fringe from the centre, (c) the distance between the 5th bright fringe on one side and the 3rd bright on the other, (d) β for 500 nm.

Show working
  1. (a) β = 600 × 10−9 × 1·2/5 × 10−3 = 1·44 × 10−4 m = 0·144 mm.
  2. (b) y10 = 10β = 1·44 × 10−3 m.
  3. (c) 5β + 3β = 8β = 1·15 × 10−3 m.
  4. (d) β ∝ λ: 1·2 × 10−4 m — narrower.

Answer 0·144 mm; 1·44 mm; 1·15 mm; 0·12 mm.

Worked exampleSlit separation from a fringe position (B23 Q14(ii))

WO-2

The 4th bright fringe is 1·5 mm from the centre with D = 1·5 m and λ = 500 nm. Find d.

Show working
  1. y4 = 4λD/d ⇒ d = 4 × 500 × 10−9 × 1·5/1·5 × 10−3 = 2·0 × 10−3 m.

Answer d = 2 mm.

Worked exampleBright or dark? (S27 Q13(i))

WO-3

At a point on the screen the path difference is 1·2 μm for light of 600 nm. Is the point bright or dark? A student says "dark, because the path difference is large". Evaluate.

Show working
  1. Δx/λ = 1·2 × 10−6/6 × 10−7 = 2·0, a whole number.
  2. Path difference 2λ: constructive interference, a bright fringe (the 2nd). The student is wrong: what matters is the path difference in wavelengths, not its size.

Answer Bright (2nd order).

Worked exampleWidth of the central maximum

WO-4

Light of 600 nm falls on a slit 0·1 mm wide; the screen is 1·5 m away. Find the angular and linear width of the central maximum.

Show working
  1. Angular width 2λ/a = 2 × 6 × 10−7/10−4 = 0·012 rad.
  2. Linear width 2λD/a = 0·018 m = 18 mm.

Answer 0·012 rad; 18 mm.

Worked exampleMaximum to minimum intensity (competency C76)

WO-5

Two coherent waves have amplitudes in the ratio 1 : 3. Find Imax : Imin.

Show working
  1. Imax/Imin = (1 + 3)2/(3 − 1)2 = 16/4 = 4·0.

Answer 4 : 1 (equivalently Imin : Imax = 1 : 4).

Worked exampleThe same apparatus under water (competency C92(d))

WO-6

The YDSE of WO-1 (β = 0·144 mm) is immersed in water, n = 1·33. Find the new fringe width.

Show working
  1. λ in water = λ/n, so β′ = β/n = 0·144/1·33 = 1·08 × 10−4 m.

Answer β′ ≈ 0·108 mm.

Worked exampleWhere bright fringes of two colours first coincide (NCERT 10.6)

WO-7

A YDSE uses 650 nm and 520 nm together, with d = 2 mm and D = 1·2 m. Find the least distance from the centre where bright fringes of both coincide.

Show working
  1. Coincide when n1(650) = n2(520); 650/520 = 5/4, so the least is n1 = 4, n2 = 5: path difference 2·6 × 10−6 m (2600 nm).
  2. y = 4 × 650 × 10−9 × 1·2/2 × 10−3 = 1·56 × 10−3 m.

Answer 1·56 mm.

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Huygens reflection with OB = O′C labelled ct: the two equal sides are the wavelet radius and the distance the far end of the wavefront travels.
  • Taking the central maximum of a single slit to have the same width as the others (it is twice as wide).
  • Counting fringes: from the 5th bright on one side to the 3rd on the other is 8β, not 2β.
  • Saying two sodium lamps give interference: they are not coherent.
  • Adding intensities instead of amplitudes when finding Imax.
  • Polarisation, Malus and Brewster: out of the 2027 syllabus.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Huygens proof (7 of 8 boards): reflection (B26, B25I, B23) or Snell’s law (B25, B24), 3 marks with a labelled figure.
  • YDSE: numerical (fringe width, positions, d from a fringe, change of λ) and the teacher–student Evaluate item on changing d, D, λ, white light or covering a slit (S27 Q13).
  • Derivation of β = λD/d (S26 Q14), and the single-slit intensity graph with the central-maximum width.
  • Wavefront one-markers (point, line, distant source; primary and secondary wavefront, wave normal), interference vs diffraction patterns from images (B26 Q15).

7. Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

Unit 7 · 7 marks · photoelectric effect, Einstein’s equation, photons, matter waves

ConceptPhotoelectric effect: what Hertz and Lenard saw

  • Light of high enough frequency ejects electrons from a metal surface. Hertz (1887): UV on the electrodes made sparks jump more easily. Lenard: the emitted particles are electrons, and they come out instantly.
  • Four facts the wave theory cannot explain: (1) below a threshold frequency ν0 nothing is emitted however intense the light; (2) the maximum kinetic energy rises linearly with ν and does not depend on intensity; (3) the photocurrent (number of electrons) is proportional to intensity; (4) emission is instantaneous (~10−9 s).
  • Stopping potential Vs: the retarding potential that just stops the fastest electrons, eVs = Kmax. Work function φ (or W0): least energy to free an electron, φ = hν0 = hc/λ0.
  • Intensity up at fixed ν: saturation current up, Vs unchanged. Frequency up at fixed intensity: Vs more negative, saturation current (about) the same.

Intensity controls how many electrons; frequency controls how fast.

ConceptPhotons and matter waves

  • Einstein extended Planck’s quanta: light is a stream of photons, each of energy hν and momentum p = E/c = h/λ, zero rest mass, speed c. One photon is absorbed wholly by one electron — all or nothing (unlike a ball, which can give part of its energy in a collision, S27 1B(iv)).
  • Wave nature: interference, diffraction (and polarisation). Particle nature: photoelectric effect. Light shows one or the other in a given experiment.
  • de Broglie: every moving particle has a wavelength λ = h/p = h/mv = h/√(2mK) = h/√(2mqV) for a charge accelerated through V. For an electron λ ≈ 1·227/√V nm.
  • Same accelerating voltage: the lightest particle (electron) has the longest λ. Same kinetic energy: λ ∝ 1/√m. λ–v is a rectangular hyperbola.
  • Davisson–Germer (qualitative): 54 eV electrons scattered from a nickel crystal show a strong peak at 50° — diffraction, with the measured λ (0·165 nm) matching de Broglie’s. Conclusion: electrons have a wave nature.
  • Planck → quantum theory of radiation; Einstein → photoelectric equation (and E = mc2); Bohr → hydrogen spectrum; de Broglie → matter waves (S27 1A(iv)).

DerivationEinstein’s photoelectric equation, and the Vs–ν graph

A photon of energy hν is absorbed by one electron at the surface.

  1. Energy conservation: part of hν frees the electron (at least φ); the rest is kinetic energy. The least-bound electrons leave with the most: Kmax = hν − φ.
  2. Emission needs Kmax ≥ 0, i.e. ν ≥ φ/h = ν0: the threshold, independent of intensity.
  3. Stopping potential: eVs = Kmax, so Vs = (h/e)ν − φ/e.
  4. This is a straight line in Vs against ν: slope h/e, ν-intercept ν0, V-intercept −φ/e.
Kmax = ½mvmax2 = hν − φ = eVs ,    Vs = heν − φe

Caution Every metal gives a line of the same slope h/e; the metal with the lower threshold gives the larger Kmax at a given ν. Planck’s constant = e × slope.

Derivationde Broglie wavelength of a particle accelerated through V

A particle of mass m and charge q starts from rest and falls through a p.d. V.

  1. Gain in kinetic energy K = qV = p2/2m.
  2. Momentum p = √(2mK) = √(2mqV).
  3. de Broglie: λ = h/p.
  4. Electron: λ = 6·63 × 10−34/√(2 × 9·11 × 10−31 × 1·6 × 10−19 V) = 1·227 × 10−9/√V m.
λ = h√2mqV = h√2mK ;   electron: λ = 1·227√V nm

Caution Ratios are the usual question: same V for e, p, d, α — λ ∝ 1/√(mq), so the electron’s is the largest. Kinetic energy ×4 halves λ.

DiagramPhotocurrent characteristics

Left: at one frequency the stopping potential is the same for every intensity; the saturation current is proportional to intensity. Right: at one intensity a higher frequency needs a larger stopping potential.

FormulaeDual nature formula sheet

QuantityFormulaNote
PhotonE = hν = hc/λ, p = h/λ = E/cE(eV) ≈ 1240/λ(nm) (1238 with h = 6·6)
EinsteinKmax = hν − φ = eVsφ = hν0 = hc/λ0
GraphVs = (h/e)ν − φ/eslope h/e
Photon fluxN = P/hν = Pλ/hcper second
de Broglieλ = h/mv = h/√(2mK) = h/√(2mqV)electron 1·227/√V nm

Worked exampleWhich metal emits, and with what energy? (B26 Q8)

DN-1

Light of wavelength 410 nm falls on metals M1 (φ = 1·9 eV) and M2 (φ = 5 eV). Which emits electrons, and what is their maximum kinetic energy?

Show working
  1. Photon energy hc/λ = 6·6 × 10−34 × 3 × 108/(410 × 10−9 × 1·6 × 10−19) = 3·02 eV.
  2. 3·02 eV > 1·9 eV but < 5·0 eV: only M1 emits.
  3. Kmax = 3·02 − 1·9 = 1·12 eV.

Answer Only M1; Kmax ≈ 1·12 eV.

Worked exampleMaximum kinetic energy and stopping potential (B23 Q15)

DN-2

Radiation of 396 nm falls on a surface of work function 1·125 eV. Find the photon energy, Kmax and Vs.

Show working
  1. E = hc/λ = 3·125 eV.
  2. Kmax = 3·125 − 1·125 = 2·00 eV.
  3. Vs = Kmax/e = 2·00 V.

Answer 3·125 eV; 2·00 eV; 2·00 V.

Worked examplePlanck’s constant from the slope (NCERT 11.5)

DN-3

The Vs–ν graph for a metal has slope 4·12 × 10−15 V s. Find h.

Show working
  1. Slope = h/e: h = 1·6 × 10−19 × 4·12 × 10−15 = 6·59 × 10−34 J s.

Answer h ≈ 6·59 × 10−34 J s.

Worked exampleThreshold wavelength and electron speed (S27 Q16)

DN-4

A surface has φ = 2·3 eV. Find its threshold wavelength. Photons of 2·8 eV fall on it: find Kmax and the maximum speed of the electrons.

Show working
  1. λ0 = hc/φ = 6·6 × 10−34 × 3 × 108/(2·3 × 1·6 × 10−19) = 5·38 × 10−7 m (538 nm, green).
  2. Kmax = 2·8 − 2·3 = 0·50 eV = 8·0 × 10−20 J.
  3. v = √(2K/m) = √(1·6 × 10−19/9·1 × 10−31) = 4·19 × 105 m s−1.

Answer λ0 ≈ 538 nm; 0·5 eV; 4·19 × 105 m s−1.

Worked examplePhoton from a hydrogen transition ejects electrons (S26 Q17, due)

DN-5

Photons from the n = 2 → 1 transition in hydrogen fall on a metal of work function 2 eV. Find the stopping potential.

Show working
  1. Photon energy 13·6(1 − 1/4) = 10·2 eV.
  2. eVs = 10·2 − 2·0: Vs = 8·2 V.

Answer 8·2 V.

Worked exampleMomentum of a photon (B26 1B(i))

DN-6

Find the momentum of a photon of energy 4·8 × 10−19 J.

Show working
  1. p = E/c = 4·8 × 10−19/3 × 108 = 1·6 × 10−27 kg m s−1.

Answer 1·6 × 10−27 kg m s−1.

Worked examplede Broglie wavelength of an electron (H16 Q12(b))

DN-7

An electron is accelerated from rest through 300 V. Find its de Broglie wavelength.

Show working
  1. λ = h/√(2meV) = 6·6 × 10−34/√(2 × 9·1 × 10−31 × 1·6 × 10−19 × 300) = 7·06 × 10−11 m.
  2. Check: 1·227/√300 = 0·0708 nm (with h = 6·63).

Answer λ ≈ 0·071 nm — X-ray size, which is why crystals diffract electrons.

Worked exampleElectron and proton with the same wavelength (S27 Q8 type)

DN-8

An electron (9·1 × 10−31 kg) and a proton (1·67 × 10−27 kg) have the same de Broglie wavelength. Compare their kinetic energies. If instead particle A has twice the wavelength of B, what is KA/KB?

Show working
  1. Same λ means the same momentum; K = p2/2m, so Ke/Kp = mp/me = 1835.
  2. Generally K = h2/2mλ2: with λA = 2λB, KA/KB = mB/4mA.

Answer The electron has about 1835 times the proton’s kinetic energy; KA : KB = mB : 4mA.

Worked examplePhotons per second from a laser (NCERT 11.4)

DN-9

A He–Ne laser emits 9·42 mW at 632·8 nm. Find the energy and momentum of each photon and the number emitted per second.

Show working
  1. E = hc/λ = 3·13 × 10−19 J; p = h/λ = 1·04 × 10−27 kg m s−1.
  2. N = P/E = 3·01 × 1016 s−1.

Answer About 3 × 1016 photons per second.

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Saying intensity changes the stopping potential or Kmax. It changes only the current.
  • Giving the slope of the Vs–ν graph as h. It is h/e; h = e × slope.
  • Drawing different slopes for different metals on the Vs–ν graph: the lines must be parallel.
  • Using λ = h/√(2mqV) with V in kV or q = e for an α-particle (q = 2e).
  • Forgetting to convert eV to joules (× 1·6 × 10−19) before using mass in kg.
  • Saying the de Broglie wavelength depends on the size of the particle (B25I 1A(iv)): it depends only on momentum.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • de Broglie 1-marker (7 of 8 boards): ratios under the same V or K, the particle with the longest λ, KA/KB from λA = 2λB (S27 Q8).
  • Photoelectric 3-marker (every current board): Einstein-equation numerical (which metal emits, Kmax, Vs) OR the Vs–ν graph with slope h/e and intercepts, two metals.
  • Effects of intensity and frequency on current, Vs and Kmax; definitions of threshold frequency, work function, stopping potential.
  • Photon momentum p = E/c; Davisson–Germer conclusion; photo-surface image question (S27 Q16); historical match (S27 1A(iv)).

8. Atoms

Unit 8(i) · with Nuclei 6 marks; Q19 (5 marks) is always this unit · α-scattering, Bohr model, energy levels, hydrogen spectrum

ConceptRutherford’s nuclear atom

  • Geiger–Marsden: α-particles on thin gold foil. Most pass straight through (atom mostly empty); a few are deflected through large angles; about 1 in 8000 is turned back by more than 90° (a tiny, massive, positive nucleus).
  • Nucleus ~10−15 m (1 fermi) against an atom ~10−10 m. The mathematical theory of scattering (impact parameter) is excluded; the distance of closest approach is in.
  • Rutherford’s model fails: an orbiting electron accelerates, should radiate continuously and spiral into the nucleus, giving a continuous spectrum — but atoms are stable and give line spectra.

ConceptBohr’s postulates and the hydrogen spectrum

  • (1) Electrons move in certain circular stationary orbits without radiating. (2) In these orbits angular momentum is quantised: mvr = nh/2π. (3) A photon is emitted or absorbed only in a jump between orbits: hν = Ei − Ef.
  • rn ∝ n2 (r1 = 0·53 Å = 0·053 nm), vn ∝ 1/n (v1 ≈ 2·2 × 106 m s−1 = c/137), En = −13·6/n2 eV.
  • K = −E, U = 2E: the total energy is negative because the electron is bound. Ionisation energy 13·6 eV; first excitation 10·2 eV.
  • Series: Lyman (to n = 1, ultraviolet), Balmer (to n = 2, visible), Paschen (n = 3), Brackett (n = 4), Pfund (n = 5), all infrared. 1/λ = R(1/nf2 − 1/ni2), R = 1·097 × 107 m−1. Use nm, not Å.
  • de Broglie’s explanation of postulate 2: a stationary orbit holds a whole number of electron waves, 2πr = nλ, which with λ = h/mv gives mvr = nh/2π.
  • Angular momentum in the 2nd orbit: 2h/2π = h/π. Limitations: only one-electron atoms; no intensities or fine structure.

r grows as n2, v falls as 1/n, E rises (towards zero) as 1/n2.

DerivationDistance of closest approach of an α-particle

An α-particle (charge 2e) with kinetic energy K heads straight for a nucleus of charge Ze.

  1. It slows as the Coulomb repulsion grows; at the distance of closest approach r0 it is momentarily at rest.
  2. All its kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy: ΔK = ΔU.
  3. ½mv2 = (1/4πε0)(2e)(Ze)/r0.
r0 = 14πε0 2Ze2K

Caution r0 sets an upper limit on the nuclear radius (~10−14 m for gold). Doubling K halves r0; r0 does not depend on the mass for a given K.

DerivationRadius and speed in the nth Bohr orbit

Electron (m, −e) in a circular orbit of radius r round a nucleus of charge Ze (Z = 1 for hydrogen).

  1. Coulomb attraction gives the centripetal force: mv2/r = kZe2/r2   ---(i)
  2. Bohr’s quantum condition: mvr = nh/2π   ---(ii)
  3. Divide (i)×r2 by (ii): v = 2πkZe2/nh = Ze2/2ε0nh.
  4. Put v back in (ii): r = nh/2πmv = ε0n2h2/πmZe2.
vn = Ze22ε0nh ∝ Zn ,    rn = ε0n2h2πmZe2 ∝ n2Z

Caution Write both Bohr equations first — that is the first mark (S27 Q19(i)(a)). For hydrogen r1 = 0·053 nm, so r3 = 9r1.

DerivationEnergy of the electron in the nth orbit, and the spectral lines

Use (i) of the previous derivation.

  1. Kinetic energy K = ½mv2 = kZe2/2r (from (i)).
  2. Potential energy U = −kZe2/r = −2K.
  3. Total E = K + U = −kZe2/2r; substitute rn.
  4. Photon in a jump ni → nf: hc/λ = Ei − Ef = (mZ2e4/8ε02h2)(1/nf2 − 1/ni2).
En = −mZ2e48ε02h2n2 = −13·6n2 eV ;   1λ = R(1nf2 − 1ni2)

Caution K = |E| and U = 2E. Shortest wavelength of a series: ni = ∞; longest: ni = nf + 1.

Worked exampleRadius of the third orbit (B25I 1B(vi) = B26 1B(vii), recycled verbatim)

AT-1

The radius of the first Bohr orbit of an atom is 0·05 nm. Find the radius of the third.

Show working
  1. r ∝ n2: r3 = 9 × 0·05 = 0·45 nm.

Answer 0·45 nm.

Worked exampleClosest approach to a gold nucleus (S26 Q19(i)(b))

AT-2

An α-particle of kinetic energy 5 MeV approaches a gold nucleus (Z = 79) head on. Find the distance of closest approach.

Show working
  1. r0 = k(2e)(Ze)/K = 9 × 109 × 2 × 79 × (1·6 × 10−19)2/(5 × 1·6 × 10−13) = 4·55 × 10−14 m.

Answer r0 ≈ 4·6 × 10−14 m.

Worked exampleShortest and longest Balmer wavelengths (B18 Q10 → B26 Q19(iii))

AT-3

Using R = 1·097 × 107 m−1, find the shortest and longest wavelengths of the Balmer series and state the region.

Show working
  1. Shortest: ∞ → 2, 1/λ = R/4: λ = 3·646 × 10−7 m (364·6 nm).
  2. Longest: 3 → 2 (Hα), 1/λ = R(1/4 − 1/9) = 5R/36: λ = 6·563 × 10−7 m (656·3 nm).
  3. Visible (the shortest lines crowd into the near UV).

Answer 364·6 nm and 656·3 nm; visible region.

Worked exampleWavelengths from an energy-level diagram (S25/S26 Q19(ii)(a))

AT-4

An atom has levels E1 = 0, E2 = 1·78 eV, E3 = 2·95 eV. Find the wavelengths of the three lines it can emit.

Show working
  1. λ = hc/ΔE with hc = 1·98 × 10−25 J m.
  2. 2 → 1: 6·95 × 10−7 m; 3 → 1: 4·19 × 10−7 m; 3 → 2 (1·17 eV): 1·06 × 10−6 m.

Answer About 695 nm (red), 420 nm (violet) and 1058 nm (infrared).

Worked exampleSpeed and energy in the ground state from the formulae

AT-5

Using the ISC constants (e = 1·6 × 10−19 C, ε0 = 8·85 × 10−12 F m−1, h = 6·6 × 10−34 J s, m = 9·1 × 10−31 kg), find the electron’s speed in the first orbit of hydrogen and its kinetic energy in eV.

Show working
  1. v1 = e2/2ε0h = (1·6 × 10−19)2/(2 × 8·85 × 10−12 × 6·6 × 10−34) = 2·19 × 106 m s−1.
  2. K = ½mv2 = 2·19 × 10−18 J = 13·7 eV (13·6 eV with unrounded constants); so E1 = −K ≈ −13·6 eV.

Answer 2·19 × 106 m s−1; K ≈ 13·7 eV with these rounded constants (13·6 eV exactly), so E1 ≈ −13·6 eV.

Worked exampleLines excited by an electron beam (NCERT 12.8)

AT-6

Hydrogen atoms in the ground state are bombarded by electrons of 12·5 eV. Which lines can be emitted? Use R = 1·097 × 107 m−1.

Show working
  1. Excitation energies: to n = 3, 13·6(1 − 1/9) = 12·09 eV; to n = 4, 12·75 eV. 12·5 eV reaches n = 3 only.
  2. Lines: 3 → 1 at 1·026 × 10−7 m, 2 → 1 at 1·215 × 10−7 m (Lyman, UV), 3 → 2 at 6·563 × 10−7 m (Balmer, red).

Answer Three lines: 102·6 nm, 121·5 nm and 656·3 nm.

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Taking K = 13·6 eV as the total energy: E1 = −13·6 eV, K = +13·6 eV, U = −27·2 eV.
  • Writing the quantum condition as mvr = nh; it is nh/2π.
  • Placing the Balmer series in the UV or Lyman in the visible.
  • Energy-level diagram with fewer than four levels, unlabelled, or with arrows pointing up for emission.
  • Using the mathematical theory of α-scattering (impact parameter): excluded.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Q19(i) derivation: vn (S27, B23) or rn (B24, B25) from the two Bohr equations, sometimes with K, U and E.
  • Scaling one-markers (r1 = 0·05 nm → r3, recycled twice), region of the Lyman and Balmer series (S27 Q19(ii)(c)), shortest Balmer line.
  • Energy-level diagram with at least four levels and a wavelength; Bohr’s postulates and the de Broglie explanation of quantisation.
  • Due from the specimens: distance of closest approach (S24–S26), photon from a transition ejecting photoelectrons (S26 Q17).

8. Nuclei

Unit 8(ii) · with Atoms 6 marks · composition, size, mass–energy, binding energy, fission and fusion

ConceptComposition and size

  • Nucleus AZX: Z protons, N = A − Z neutrons. Isotopes: same Z (1H, 2H, 3H). Isobars: same A (40Ar, 40Ca). Isotones: same N (13C, 14N, each 7 neutrons).
  • Unified atomic mass unit 1 u = 1/12 of the mass of a 12C atom = 1·66 × 10−27 kg = 931·5 MeV/c2.
  • Radius R = R0A1/3, R0 ≈ 1·2 fm. Volume ∝ A and mass ∝ A, so the density (~2·3 × 1017 kg m−3) is the same for all nuclei.
  • Nuclear force: strongest of the four, short-range (~2–3 fm), charge-independent, attractive (repulsive below ~0·8 fm).

ConceptMass defect, binding energy and the BE/A curve

  • Mass defect Δm = [ZmH + Nmn] − M (atomic masses, so the electrons cancel). Binding energy BE = Δm c2 = Δm(u) × 931·5 MeV.
  • BE/A rises steeply for light nuclei (with peaks at 4He, 12C, 16O), is flat at about 8–8·8 MeV for 30 < A < 170 with a maximum at 56Fe (most stable), and falls to about 7·6 MeV for uranium.
  • So energy is released by fusing light nuclei (moving up the steep left side) or fissioning heavy ones (moving to the middle).
  • Pair production: a γ-photon of at least 2mec2 = 1·02 MeV, near a nucleus (to conserve momentum), becomes e− + e+; annihilation: e− + e+ → 2γ (two 0·511 MeV photons in opposite directions; PET scanning). For p p̄: 2 × 938·3 = 1876·6 MeV.

A larger binding energy per nucleon means a more stable nucleus, not a larger total BE.

ConceptFission, fusion and the reactor

  • Fission: 235U + 1n → 141Ba + 92Kr + 3 1n + ~200 MeV. The released neutrons can cause further fissions: a chain reaction, controlled (reactor) or uncontrolled (bomb). Details of the chain reaction are not required.
  • Reactor parts: fuel rods (enriched U-235); moderator (heavy water or graphite) slows the fast neutrons, which are then more likely to cause fission; control rods (cadmium or boron) absorb neutrons — pushed in fully for an emergency shut-down; coolant (water, heavy water, liquid sodium) carries the heat to the heat exchanger and turbine; concrete/lead shielding and a steel casing. Critical: on average one neutron per fission causes another (k = 1).
  • Fusion: 4 1H → 4He + 2e+ + 2ν + 26·7 MeV, the source of the Sun’s energy. Needs ~107 K (the syllabus says ~106 degrees) so that nuclei beat the Coulomb barrier: thermonuclear. Hydrogen bomb: a fission bomb supplies the temperature.

Derivation1 u = 931·5 MeV

1 u = 1·6605 × 10−27 kg (1/12 of a 12C atom).

  1. E = mc2 = 1·6605 × 10−27 × (2·998 × 108)2 = 1·4924 × 10−10 J.
  2. 1 MeV = 1·6022 × 10−13 J, so E = 1·4924 × 10−10/1·6022 × 10−13 MeV.
1 u × c2 = 931·5 MeV

Caution With the rounded ISC values (1·66 × 10−27, 3 × 108, 1·6 × 10−19) the same sum gives about 934 MeV; the key (S27 Q19(i)(b)) accepts the working and quotes 931·5 MeV.

DerivationNuclear density is independent of A

Nucleus of mass number A, radius R = R0A1/3; each nucleon of mass m ≈ 1 u.

  1. Mass M = Am.
  2. Volume V = (4/3)πR3 = (4/3)πR03A.
  3. ρ = M/V: the A cancels.
ρ = 3m4πR03 ≈ 2·3 × 1017 kg m−3, the same for every nucleus

Caution This is NCERT 13.10, set as S27 Q19(ii)(a). The ratio of two radii is (A1/A2)1/3.

DerivationEnergy released when a heavy nucleus splits (syllabus calculation)

A nucleus with A = 240 and BE/A ≈ 7·6 MeV splits into two with A = 120 and BE/A ≈ 8·5 MeV.

  1. Binding energy before: 240 × 7·6 = 1824 MeV.
  2. After: 2 × 120 × 8·5 = 2040 MeV.
  3. The products are more tightly bound; the difference is released as kinetic energy of the fragments and neutrons.
Q = 2040 − 1824 = 216 MeV ≈ 200 MeV per fission

Caution Q = (total BE of the products) − (total BE of the reactants) = (mass of the reactants − mass of the products) × 931·5 MeV/u.

DiagramThe reactor and pair production

Worked exampleMass converted in a bomb (competency C61)

A bomb releases the energy of 30 kilotonnes of TNT (4 × 109 J t−1). How much mass is converted?

  1. E = 3 × 104 × 4 × 109 = 1·2 × 1014 J.
  2. m = E/c2 = 1·2 × 1014/9 × 1016 = 1·33 × 10−3 kg.

Answer About 1·33 g.

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Using nuclear masses for the nucleus and mp for the protons inconsistently: with atomic masses use mH = 1·007825 u.
  • Radioactive decay law, half-life and mean life: not in the 2027 syllabus.
  • Saying the moderator absorbs neutrons (that is the control rods); the moderator slows them.
  • Pair production in free space: it needs a nucleus nearby to take up momentum.
  • Drawing the BE/A curve with its maximum at uranium, or without marking Fe-56 and the fission and fusion regions.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Q19 (5 marks) pairs a Bohr derivation with 1 u = 931·5 MeV (S27) or nuclear density (S27 Q19(ii)(a)), or BE/A graph with regions, or a mass-defect / Q-value numerical.
  • Isotopes, isobars and isotones with examples (S27 Q19(ii)(b)).
  • Reactor parts and their functions, fission vs fusion, thermonuclear energy in the Sun (7 of 8 boards).
  • Pair production / annihilation energy (6 of 8 boards; S27 1B(v) asks for the p p̄ threshold).

9. Electronic Devices

Unit 9 · 7 marks; the Q20 passage is on electronics in about half the papers · energy bands, p-n junction, rectifiers, Zener, LED, photodiode, solar cell

ConceptEnergy bands and semiconductors

  • In a solid the discrete levels of isolated atoms (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, …) split into bands of closely spaced levels separated by forbidden gaps. Valence band: the highest filled band; conduction band: the next one up.
  • Conductor: bands overlap (or the conduction band is partly filled) — no forbidden gap. Semiconductor: small gap (Ge 0·7 eV, Si 1·1 eV). Insulator: large gap (diamond, C, ~5–6 eV). (Eg)C > Si > Ge.
  • In a semiconductor, heat breaks covalent bonds: electrons go to the conduction band leaving holes. Resistance therefore falls as temperature rises (the opposite of a metal).
  • Intrinsic: pure, ne = nh. Extrinsic: doped. n-type — pentavalent donor (P, As, Sb), majority electrons, donor level just below the conduction band. p-type — trivalent acceptor (B, Al, In, Ga), majority holes, acceptor level just above the valence band. Either type is electrically neutral.

No forbidden band at all means a metal (S27 Q17(iii), recycled from B25).

ConceptThe p-n junction diode

  • At the junction electrons diffuse into p and holes into n; they recombine and leave behind immobile ions (− on the p side, + on the n side). This depletion region (~1 μm) has no free carriers; its ions set up a field from n to p and a potential barrier (~0·7 V for Si, 0·3 V for Ge) which stops further diffusion.
  • Forward bias (p to +): the barrier and the depletion width shrink, majority carriers cross, current rises steeply beyond the knee voltage (mA). Reverse bias (p to −): barrier and width grow; only a tiny, nearly constant current of minority carriers flows (μA) until breakdown.
  • Symbol: the arrow points the way conventional current flows in forward bias. Dynamic resistance = ΔV/ΔI from the graph. A microammeter is used to measure the reverse current.

ConceptSpecial diodes

  • Zener: heavily doped, designed to work in reverse breakdown; the voltage across it stays at VZ over a wide range of current — a voltage regulator.
  • Photodiode: operated in reverse bias; light of hν > Eg makes electron–hole pairs near the junction and the reverse current rises with intensity (the change is a large fraction of the small dark current). Light detectors, rain sensors, optical communication.
  • LED: forward biased; electrons and holes recombine at the junction and emit photons of energy ~Eg (colour set by the band gap: GaAsP red/yellow, GaN blue). Advantages: low voltage and power, long life, fast switching, no warm-up, and they save energy without pollution or contributing to global warming (syllabus).
  • Solar cell: a p-n junction with no external bias and a large, thin, illuminated front; light generates pairs, the junction field separates them (electrons to n, holes to p) and an emf (~0·5–0·6 V) appears. Its I–V curve lies in the fourth quadrant. Best material Eg ~1–1·8 eV (Si, GaAs). Light energy → electrical energy.
  • Photon energy against gap: E > Eg creates pairs (excess becomes heat); E < Eg does nothing.

DiagramEnergy bands and doping

DerivationFormation of the depletion region and potential barrier

A p-type and an n-type region are formed in one crystal.

  1. Concentration difference: holes diffuse from p to n and electrons from n to p (diffusion current).
  2. Each carrier that crosses recombines near the junction, leaving an uncovered ion: negative acceptor ions on the p side, positive donor ions on the n side.
  3. These fixed charges set up a field directed from n to p, which opposes further diffusion and drives minority carriers across (drift current).
  4. Equilibrium: drift balances diffusion; the region is depleted of free carriers.
Depletion region with a potential barrier V0 (Si ~0·7 V), n side at the higher potential

Caution In forward bias the applied field opposes the barrier field, so the barrier falls (C38 asks you to draw this).

DerivationForward and reverse bias and the I–V characteristic

Connect the diode to a variable dc supply with a voltmeter across it and a milliammeter (microammeter in reverse) in series.

  1. Forward: almost no current until the applied voltage overcomes the barrier (knee ~0·7 V for Si); then the current rises steeply.
  2. Reverse: the barrier grows; only minority carriers cross, giving a tiny saturation current almost independent of V.
  3. At a large reverse voltage (breakdown) the current rises suddenly.
Non-ohmic: low resistance forward, very high resistance reverse

Caution Use different scales for the two halves (mA and V forward, μA reverse) and say so on the graph.

DerivationHalf-wave rectifier

The ac supply is applied through a transformer to a diode in series with a load RL.

  1. Positive half-cycle: A is positive, D is forward-biased and conducts; current flows through RL.
  2. Negative half-cycle: D is reverse-biased; no current.
  3. The output is a series of positive half-waves: pulsating dc.
Output frequency = input frequency (50 Hz in, 50 Hz out); only one half-cycle of the input is used

Caution Each component: the transformer sets the voltage, the diode rectifies, RL is where the output is taken.

DerivationFull-wave rectifier (centre-tap)

The secondary is centre-tapped (C); diodes D1 and D2 connect its two ends A and B to one end of RL, the other end going to C.

  1. Positive half-cycle (A positive with respect to C): D1 conducts, D2 is reverse-biased; current through RL from the diode end towards C.
  2. Negative half-cycle (B positive with respect to C): D2 conducts, D1 is off; the current in RL flows in the same direction.
  3. Both halves of the input appear across RL in the same direction.
Output frequency = 2 × input frequency (50 Hz in, 100 Hz out); more efficient than half-wave

Caution The bridge rectifier (four diodes) is excluded from the syllabus; draw the centre-tap circuit.

DerivationZener diode as a voltage regulator

The Zener is reverse-biased in parallel with the load RL, fed from an unregulated supply through a series resistor Rs.

  1. In breakdown the Zener voltage stays at VZ whatever the current through it.
  2. If the input rises, the current through Rs rises; the extra current goes through the Zener and the extra voltage drops across Rs. VZ, and so the load voltage, is unchanged.
  3. If the input falls, the Zener current falls, again keeping VL = VZ.
VL = VZ ;   Is = (Vin − VZ)/Rs = IZ + IL

Caution Rs is essential: without it the Zener current is unlimited.

DerivationSolar cell and photodiode: working and characteristics

Both are p-n junctions whose junction region is exposed to light.

  1. Generation: photons with hν > Eg create electron–hole pairs near the junction.
  2. Separation: the junction field sweeps electrons to the n side and holes to the p side.
  3. Solar cell (no bias): the separated charges build up an open-circuit emf Voc; on a load they drive a current, the short-circuit value Isc being proportional to intensity. Photodiode (reverse bias): the separated carriers add to the reverse current, which grows with intensity.
Solar cell: light → electrical energy, I–V in the 4th quadrant. Photodiode: reverse current ∝ intensity

Caution Why reverse bias for a photodiode: the fractional change in the tiny reverse current is large, so it is easy to detect.

Answer 50 Hz and 100 Hz.

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Drawing the bridge rectifier: excluded; use the centre-tap circuit.
  • Saying the reverse current is due to majority carriers; it is due to minority carriers.
  • Forward-biasing a photodiode or reverse-biasing an LED.
  • Calling an n-type semiconductor negatively charged: it is neutral.
  • Saying a semiconductor’s resistance rises with temperature.
  • Transistors, logic gates and communication systems: not in the 2027 syllabus.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Rectifier with waveforms (5 of 8 boards): full-wave centre-tap (B23 Q17, B25 Q20) or half-wave (B26 Q20(iv)); output frequency.
  • Bias effects on depletion width, barrier and resistance (S27 1A(v)); why the reverse current is tiny (S27 Q7(i)); depletion region and barrier defined (S23 Q8 → B24 Q8).
  • Energy bands: conductor / semiconductor / insulator; "no forbidden band → metal" (verbatim recycle); resistance vs temperature; n- and p-type dopants and majority carriers.
  • Solar cell working and I–V (S27 Q17), LED advantages and colour (S26 Q20), photodiode biasing (S24 Q20); Zener symbol, I–V and regulator.
